scenes.text: Khushwant Singh recalls his grandmother: old, wrinkled, always praying with her rosary.
As he grows up and moves to the city, their friendship slowly changes.
On the day of her death, the sparrows she fed sit silently around her body.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An autobiographical sketch by **Khushwant Singh** (1915–2014), journalist and writer. He paints a loving, humorous and finally moving portrait of his grandmother, tracing three stages of their relationship: village, city, and his return from abroad.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: In the village the author lived with his grandmother. She woke him, bathed and dressed him, and walked with him to the temple school, reciting prayers. While he learned, she read scriptures; on the way back they threw stale chapattis to the village dogs. They were close friends.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: When the family moved to the city, he went to an English school in a motor bus. She could no longer help with lessons; she disliked that he learnt science and music ('music was for harlots and beggars'). Given her own room, she spent her time spinning and feeding sparrows. When he left for university abroad she saw him off silently, praying.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Five years later she welcomed him back. That evening, for the first time, she ignored her prayers and sang homecoming songs, beating an old drum. Next morning she fell ill, refused to stop praying, and died peacefully with her lips moving in prayer. Thousands of sparrows sat silently around her body and flew away after it was carried off; they ignored the bread crumbs thrown to them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

scenes.text: A student asks: what is this text really about, beyond what happens?
Themes and characters answer that question — and they carry the most marks in long answers.

steps.title: Theme: Love across generations
steps.body: The bond between child and grandparent survives distance and changing interests, even when they can no longer share daily life.

steps.title: Theme: Tradition versus modernity
steps.body: Her objections to English education, science and music show the gap between her religious, village world and his modern, urban one.

steps.title: Theme: Dignity in old age and death
steps.body: She accepts death calmly, praying to the end — a picture of serenity and faith.

steps.title: Character sketch: The grandmother
steps.body: She is short, fat, slightly bent, with a face criss-crossed with wrinkles. She prays constantly, loves feeding animals and birds, and keeps her dignity. Her love for the author is quiet; her only show of emotion is the singing on his return.

steps.title: Character sketch: The author (narrator)
steps.body: He finds it hard to believe she was ever young and pretty, describes her with gentle humour, and frankly admits their friendship faded in the city.

steps.title: Character sketch: The sparrows
steps.body: Her daily companions; their silent mourning shows how much she was loved by all living things.

steps.title: Style & literary devices
steps.body:
- **Simile:** she was 'like the winter landscape in the mountains, an expanse of pure white serenity'.
- **Humour:** the idea of her being young and pretty seemed 'almost revolting'.
- **Imagery:** the sparrows sitting silently on the verandah.
- First-person, gently ironic narration.

steps.title: Q: What were the three stages in the author's relationship with his grandmother?
steps.body: **Village:** they were inseparable friends — she prepared him for school and accompanied him. **City:** they shared a room but she could not help with English lessons; the friendship weakened. **University and after:** he had his own room and the 'common link of friendship was snapped', yet she still loved him, as her singing on his return proved.

steps.title: Q: Why did the grandmother dislike the author's music lessons?
steps.body: She associated music with 'harlots and beggars' and thought it unsuitable for gentlefolk. Her objection shows her traditional values; she expressed displeasure by silence rather than argument.

steps.title: Q: How did the sparrows express sorrow at her death?
steps.body: Thousands of sparrows sat scattered on the verandah and in her room in silence; they did not chirp and ignored the crumbs the author's mother threw. When her body was carried away they flew off quietly — a touching sign of her bond with them.

steps.body:
- Open with a direct answer in one line.
- Support it with a specific moment or detail from the text.
- Keep to the word limit; end with a link to the theme.

story.title: A storm in the Indian Ocean

scenes.text: A family sails round the world in their boat Wavewalker.
A giant wave smashes the boat; water pours in, and the captain is hurt.
With courage and teamwork they find a tiny island — and survive.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A first-person account of a real voyage by the narrator (a sailor), his wife Mary, son Jonathan and daughter Suzanne, with two crewmen. It celebrates courage, optimism and teamwork in the face of disaster in the southern Indian Ocean.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: The family set out from Plymouth, England, in July 1976 in the 23-metre, 30-ton boat *Wavewalker*, to repeat Captain Cook's round-the-world voyage. They hired two crewmen, Larry Vigil and Herb Seigler, to help in rough seas. After Cape Town they sailed east towards Australia and met huge waves.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: On 2 January, a gigantic wave struck. The narrator was thrown overboard and dragged back; the deck was smashed, water flooded in, and his ribs were broken. Mary steered; the narrator and the crew pumped water for hours. Suzanne had a head injury but stayed quiet so as not to worry them. Jonathan said they were not afraid to die if they could all be together.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Repairs held; the narrator calculated the position of the tiny Île Amsterdam using a compass and charts. On 5 January, Jonathan sighted the island ('Daddy, you're the best daddy in the whole world'). They anchored and were helped ashore by the island's inhabitants. The narrator credits the courage of his wife, crew and children.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

steps.title: Theme: Courage in crisis
steps.body: Adults and children alike act bravely: no one panics, everyone works.

steps.title: Theme: Optimism and family love
steps.body: The title sums it up: fear of death disappears when the family is together.

steps.title: Theme: Teamwork and skill
steps.body: Navigation, steering, pumping and repair all had to work — survival depended on everyone.

steps.title: Character sketch: The narrator
steps.body: Despite broken ribs he directs repairs and navigates by dead reckoning to a speck of an island.

steps.title: Character sketch: Mary
steps.body: She steers the boat through the storm and keeps calm.

steps.title: Character sketch: Sue (Suzanne)
steps.body: Badly hurt on the head, she hides her pain and makes a card for her parents.

steps.title: Character sketch: Jonathan
steps.body: Says the family is not afraid to die together, and sights the island first.

steps.title: Style & literary devices
steps.body:
- Vivid first-person narration in chronological order with dates.
- Nautical vocabulary: *jib, deck, hatch, pump, storm jib, mainmast*.
- Short sentences build suspense in the storm scenes.

steps.title: Q: What difference did the narrator notice in the children during the crisis?
steps.body: The children behaved with surprising maturity. Jonathan said he was not afraid to die as long as they were together; Sue hid a serious head injury so as not to burden anyone and made a card thanking her parents. Their courage strengthened the adults.

steps.title: Q: How did the narrator find Île Amsterdam?
steps.body: Without modern aids, he used his remaining navigation skills — compass bearings, speed estimates and charts — to calculate the island's position, then steered for it. When it appeared on the horizon, Jonathan's cheer confirmed his success.

steps.title: Q: What does the title tell us about the story?
steps.body: It shows that love and togetherness can overcome fear of death. In the worst moment, the family's unity gave them courage to fight on — and survive.

scenes.text: In the Valley of the Kings, Egypt, a mummy lies in a dark tomb.
In 2005 a portable CT scanner arrives to look inside without damaging it.
Could modern science solve the mystery of how the boy king died?

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An informative article by A. R. Williams about Tutankhamun, the teenage pharaoh of ancient Egypt, and the 2005 CT scan of his mummy led by Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass. It links history, archaeology and technology.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Tutankhamun ruled Egypt over 3,300 years ago and died at about nineteen. His tomb was discovered in 1922 by British archaeologist Howard Carter. Its treasures were spectacular, but the resins used in burial had hardened, cementing the mummy to the coffin; Carter's team cut and chiselled the body apart to remove it, damaging it.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Tut's father or grandfather Amenhotep III was a powerful king; Akhenaten (possibly his father) promoted worship of the Aten (sun disk). Tut restored the old gods. His early death left mysteries: illness? murder? an accident?

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: On 5 January 2005 the mummy was taken out and passed through a portable CT scanner in a trailer near the tomb. The scan produced 1,700 digital X-ray images in cross-section, letting scientists study the body without harm. Hawass declared it a success after a cooler fan problem was solved. The project aimed to settle questions about his age and death and to create a forensic reconstruction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

steps.title: Q: Why was Carter's team forced to cut the mummy?
steps.body: Ritual resins poured over the body had hardened like cement, fixing it to the gold coffin. When sun-heating failed, they cut the mummy apart — limbs and head removed — to extract it, causing damage.

steps.title: Q: What is a CT scan and why was it useful here?
steps.body: Computed tomography takes hundreds of X-ray cross-sections and combines them into a 3-D image. It let scientists examine Tut's bones and body without opening or harming the fragile mummy.

steps.title: Q: How does the article connect past and present?
steps.body: It sets the burial rituals of 3,300 years ago beside a twenty-first-century scanner, showing how modern science continues the 'saga' of discovery.

courses.title: Hornbill · The Ailing Planet: the Green Movement's Role
courses.summary: The essay begins with the shift to a holistic view of Earth as a living organism whose needs must be respected. The Brundtland Commission's idea of **sustainable development** — meeting present needs without compromising future generations…

scenes.text: Imagine Earth as a patient whose health is worsening.
Forests vanish, fisheries collapse, deserts spread.
The writer asks: can humans become trustees of the planet, not owners?

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An essay by **Nani Palkhivala** (1920–2002), jurist and economist, first published in *The Indian Express* (1994). It argues that environmental damage is a threat to human survival and supports the 'green movement'.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: The essay begins with the shift to a holistic view of Earth as a living organism whose needs must be respected. The Brundtland Commission's idea of **sustainable development** — meeting present needs without compromising future generations — is central.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: The earth's four principal biological systems — **fisheries, forests, grasslands and croplands** — are being over-used. When human claims exceed their sustainable yield, they get damaged. Forests are disappearing (deforestation in developing countries), and population growth worsens poverty and pressure on resources.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Palkhivala stresses that 'development is the best contraceptive', yet population control is urgent. He cites the idea that we have 'not inherited this earth from our parents; we have borrowed it from our children'. He closes by urging humans to see themselves as trustees of the planet and asks whether we will act in time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

courses.summary: Professor Gaitonde, a historian, plans to research after a train journey to Bombay. Earlier he had discussed with physicist Rajendra Deshpande the idea of alternative histories. On the way he has a collision with a truck and loses…

scenes.text: Professor Gaitonde boards a train to Bombay — and wakes up in a different India.
Here, the Marathas won the Battle of Panipat in 1761, and the British never ruled.
Rajendra Deshpande explains it with physics: catastrophe theory and quantum reality.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A science-fiction story by astrophysicist **Jayant Narlikar**. It explores 'alternative history' — what if the Marathas had won the Third Battle of Panipat (1761)? — and explains it with catastrophe theory and the lack of certainty in quantum mechanics.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Professor Gaitonde, a historian, plans to research after a train journey to Bombay. Earlier he had discussed with physicist Rajendra Deshpande the idea of alternative histories. On the way he has a collision with a truck and loses consciousness.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: He finds himself in a Bombay where the East India Company is only a trading company; India was never colonised because the Marathas won at Panipat under Vishwasrao and Bhausaheb. In a library he reads a history book that confirms this. At a public meeting at Azad Maidan, he objects that the chair is empty and takes it himself — and is thrown out.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Back in his world, he tells Rajendra. Rajendra explains through **catastrophe theory** (small causes changing outcomes at critical points) and quantum theory's idea of many possible realities: at Panipat, Vishwasrao narrowly escaped a bullet in Gaitonde's experience; in reality he was killed. Gaitonde, at the moment of the collision, may have 'crossed over' between worlds. The theory explains his adventure but keeps the mystery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

scenes.text: A writer drives from Lhasa across the Tibetan plateau with driver Tsetan.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A travelogue by **Nick Middleton**, from his book *Travels as a Brief Visitor*. It describes his journey across Tibet towards Mount Kailash, and the land, people and hardships of high altitude.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Leaving Ravu with driver Tsetan and companion Daniel, the author heads towards Mount Kailash. They pass nomads' tents guarded by fierce Tibetan mastiffs and cross high passes. To avoid snowed-in routes Tsetan takes shortcuts across rough land; Daniel leaves at Lhatse to return.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: At high altitude the author suffers a headache, a blocked nose and sleepless nights. They pass through Hor, a bleak, dirty town on Lake Mansarovar, disappointing compared with poetic descriptions of the sacred lake.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: They reach Darchen, starting point of the pilgrimage around (kora) Mount Kailash, where a doctor at the medical clinic diagnoses a cold aggravated by altitude and gives him pills. He meets Norbu, a Tibetan scholar working in Beijing, who suggests they do the kora together. The journey ends with the author excited to begin his pilgrimage.

scenes.text: A poet looks at a cardboard photograph of her mother as a girl, on a beach with two cousins.
The sea is unchanged; the girl has grown, aged and died.
The poet says: 'its silence silences'.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by **Shirley Toulson** in three stanzas. Through one photograph it reflects on time, memory, loss and the permanence of nature compared with human life.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: **Stanza 1:** The cardboard shows the poet's mother, about twelve, on a seaside holiday, with her two girl cousins holding her hands, all paddling and smiling for an uncle who took the picture.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: **Stanza 2:** The sea, which the poet calls 'unchanged', still washes the same shore; but the girl's face has changed with time. Years later the mother would laugh at the photo, remembering 'Betty and Dolly' and how they were dressed for the beach. The sea holiday was her past; the mother's laughter is now the poet's past.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: **Stanza 3:** The mother has been dead for twelve years (the same span as her age in the photo). The poet says there is nothing to say about the situation: 'its silence silences' — grief leaves her wordless.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a story-style summary instead of explaining lines with their poetic meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the line that shows it.
- Forgetting the poet's name and the central idea in the opening line of an answer.

scenes.text: On a soft, falling evening the poet asks the rain: who are you?
The rain replies: I am the Poem of Earth.
It rises from earth and returns to it — like a song from its poet.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by **Walt Whitman** (1819–1892), American poet, written as a dialogue between the poet and the rain. It describes the water cycle and compares it to the life of a song.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: The poet asks the soft-falling shower who it is. The rain answers that it is the 'Poem of Earth'. It rises 'impalpable' from land and the 'bottomless sea' as vapour, forms clouds, and comes down to wash the drouths and dust of the earth.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Falling, it gives life to seeds that would otherwise lie 'latent, unborn'. By day and night it gives back life to its own origin, making it 'pure and beautiful'.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: In brackets the poet adds: 'For song, issuing from its birth-place, after fulfilment, wandering, / Reck'd or unreck'd, duly with love returns.' A song, like rain, comes from the poet's heart, travels to people, and returns to its maker whether it is appreciated or not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a story-style summary instead of explaining lines with their poetic meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the line that shows it.
- Forgetting the poet's name and the central idea in the opening line of an answer.

steps.title: Q: Why does the rain call itself 'the Poem of Earth'?
steps.body: Like a poem, it is beautiful and gives meaning and life. It rises from the earth and returns to enrich it, just as a poem rises from a poet's heart.

steps.title: Summary — part 3

scenes.text: A father feels he doesn't know his grown son, though they live together.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by **Elizabeth Jennings** (1926–2001), British poet. A father expresses the pain of a generation gap and his longing to understand his son.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: The father says he does not understand his son, though they have lived in the same house for years. He knows nothing of him; he cannot find common ground. He wishes to build 'from the land' — from his own seed — a bond again.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: He says the son has grown up 'of my own seed', yet seems a stranger. The son has his own world and speaks a different language of feeling. The father wishes he could have a life like his son's, but cannot; neither can share.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: He admits silence surrounds them; both are wounded. He wishes for mutual forgiveness and love: 'I'd have us share… / Forgive me, I'd say, and we'd both forgive.' The poem ends in hope and uncertainty.

steps.body:
- Writing a story-style summary instead of explaining lines with their poetic meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the line that shows it.
- Forgetting the poet's name and the central idea in the opening line of an answer.

scenes.text: At four in the morning, cousin Mourad rides up on a beautiful white horse.
Aram, nine, longs to ride — but the Garoghlanian tribe is famous for honesty.
Can a 'borrowed' horse be returned before anyone finds out?

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A story by **William Saroyan** (Armenian-American) about two boys of the poor but honest Garoghlanian family in California, and a horse they 'borrow'. It explores honesty, innocence and the longing of childhood.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Aram, aged nine, is woken at 4 a.m. by his cousin Mourad, thirteen, sitting on a beautiful white horse. Aram knows they are too poor to buy a horse, and their tribe is famous for honesty, so Mourad cannot have stolen it — yet he has taken it. Aram decides it is not stealing as long as they don't sell it.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: They ride in the country; Mourad has 'a way with animals', but Aram falls when he rides alone. They hide the horse in the barn of a deserted vineyard. John Byro, an Assyrian farmer, tells Aram's family that his white horse was stolen a month ago.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Uncle Khosrove, who always says 'It is no harm; pay no attention to it', dismisses Byro's worry. Weeks later the boys meet John Byro while riding; he looks at the horse's teeth and says it is like his own, but 'I would swear it is my horse if I didn't know your parents'. Next morning the boys return the horse; Byro later finds it improved in temper and stronger.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

The boys return the horse to Byro's barn

scenes.text: A student asks: what is this text really about, beyond what happens?
Themes and characters answer that question — and they carry the most marks in long answers.

steps.title: Theme: Honesty and trust
steps.body: The family's reputation makes Byro trust them; the boys return the horse.

steps.title: Theme: Innocence and desire
steps.body: A child's longing to ride outweighs his sense of right for a while.

steps.title: Theme: Community values
steps.body: Respect for family name shapes behaviour.

steps.title: Character sketch: Aram
steps.body: His logic that 'borrowing' is not stealing shows childish innocence.

steps.title: Character sketch: Mourad
steps.body: Takes the horse but cares for it and returns it.

steps.title: Character sketch: John Byro
steps.body: Recognises his horse but trusts the family's honesty.

steps.title: Character sketch: Uncle Khosrove
steps.body: 'It is no harm; pay no attention to it.'

steps.title: Style & literary devices
steps.body:
- First-person narration with humour.

scenes.text: After the war, a young woman returns to an address her mother gave her.
Inside, she sees her family's cutlery, tablecloth and furniture.
She decides to forget the address.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A story by **Marga Minco** (Dutch writer) set after World War II. A Jewish girl's family entrusted their possessions to an acquaintance, Mrs Dorling, before persecution. It explores loss, memory and moving on.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: During the war Mrs Dorling, an old acquaintance, kept taking the mother's valuables 'to save them'. The mother gave her daughter the address: Marconistraat number 46. The mother later died; the daughter survived.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: After liberation the narrator goes to the address. Mrs Dorling opens the door wearing her mother's green knitted cardigan, says she has no time and refuses to let her in. On a second visit Mrs Dorling's daughter lets her in.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: In the living room she sees the familiar objects — the Hanukkah candlestick, the antique pewter plates, the tablecloth with a burn mark, the cutlery — but displaced in strange surroundings they feel worthless. She leaves, deciding to forget the address, since the objects are linked to a past that no longer exists.

scenes.text: Mrs Pearson is the unpaid servant of her selfish family.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A one-act play by **J. B. Priestley** (English dramatist). A humorous satire on the way housewives are taken for granted, with a magical personality swap.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Mrs Annie Pearson waits on her husband George and grown children Doris and Cyril, who treat her like a servant. Her bold neighbour Mrs Fitzgerald, a fortune-teller, says she must stand up for herself and proposes swapping bodies through an Oriental spell.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: In Mrs Pearson's body, Mrs Fitzgerald smokes, plays cards, refuses to cook, and insults Doris (her boyfriend Charlie Spence), Cyril and George, revealing that the club members laugh at George behind his back. The family is shocked.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: The personalities are swapped back. The real Mrs Pearson, now firmer, enjoys her family's new politeness; they agree to stay at home and play rummy with her while she prepares supper — and she asks for help.

story.title: A king, an arch and a melon

scenes.text: A 'just and placid' king orders an arch built across a thoroughfare.
He bumps his head on it — and seeks someone to hang.
Through silly logic, a melon ends up crowned king.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A humorous narrative poem by **Vikram Seth**, satirising foolish rulers, blind justice and mob mentality.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: A just and placid king orders an arch to be built across a thoroughfare 'to edify the spectators'. Built too low, it knocks off his crown. He orders the chief of builders hanged.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Blame passes from builders to workmen to masons to the architect, who blames the king's own changes. The wise man, consulted, says the arch itself is guilty — but it touched the king's head and cannot be hanged. Finally, the crowd wants a hanging; the noose is too high for all except the king, who is the only one tall enough — so the king is hanged.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: By custom, the next man to pass the city gate chooses the new king. An idiot passes and says 'A melon', so a melon is crowned. The people don't mind as long as they are left in peace and freedom; when asked, they say, 'Long live the King!' The city is called Melon City.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the story without linking it to the question asked.
- Mixing up who says or does what — reread the key scene.
- Writing the theme as a one-word label without evidence from the text.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Entrepreneur:** a person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources and bears the risk to start a venture. **Entrepreneurship:** the process of creating and running it.
Traits: initiative, risk-taking (calculated), creativity, persistence, leadership, ability to spot opportunity, decision-making, self-confidence, networking.
Entrepreneur vs manager: entrepreneur takes risks and innovates for profit and growth; manager runs operations for an owner and is salaried.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Is a shop owner who copies a neighbour's business an entrepreneur? Yes, if she takes initiative and bears risk; an *innovative* entrepreneur adds something new such as home delivery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating entrepreneur with a large business owner only.
- Saying entrepreneurs avoid all risk; they manage *calculated* risk.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **By size (MSME in India):** micro, small, medium enterprises defined by investment and turnover. Following the 2020 revision, micro: investment up to ₹1 crore and turnover up to ₹5 crore; small: up to ₹10 crore and ₹50 crore; medium: up to ₹50 crore and ₹250 crore.
- **By form:** sole proprietorship, partnership, LLP, company, cooperative.
- **By activity:** manufacturing, service, trading.
- **Sources of ideas:** own problems, hobbies, market gaps, trends, customer complaints, technology change, existing products improved, government schemes.
- Tools: brainstorming, SWOT, observing customers.

steps.title: Solved example

steps.title: Common mistake

scenes.text: A loan officer asks Meera for her plan: who will buy, how much, at what price and how the loan will be repaid.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
A **business plan** is a written roadmap: executive summary, business description, market analysis, marketing plan, operations plan, management team, financial plan (investment, projected income, break-even), risk analysis.
**Market research:** primary (surveys, interviews, observation) and secondary (reports, census, websites). Define the **target market**, size, competitors and customer needs.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Market size: 2,000 households in a locality; survey says 25% would buy weekly. Potential buyers = 2,000 × 0.25 = **500 households**. If each buys ₹300 per month, potential monthly sales = 500 × 300 = **₹1,50,000**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Writing a plan without evidence about customers; guess-based sales forecasts mislead.

scenes.text: Arjun makes scented candles: rent and equipment are fixed, wax and wicks vary with output.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Fixed cost (FC):** does not change with output (rent). **Variable cost (VC):** changes with output (materials).
- Total cost = FC + VC × units.
- Revenue = price × units. Profit = Revenue − Total cost.
- **Contribution per unit** = selling price − variable cost per unit.
- **Break-even units = FC ÷ contribution per unit.** Break-even revenue = units × price.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
FC = ₹12,000 per month; price = ₹150; VC = ₹90 per candle.
- Contribution = 150 − 90 = ₹60.
- Break-even = 12,000 ÷ 60 = **200 candles**; revenue at break-even = 200 × 150 = **₹30,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing fixed cost by price instead of contribution.
- Treating all costs as variable.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Marketing:** identifying and satisfying customer needs profitably.
**Marketing mix (4Ps):** **Product** (quality, design, brand, packaging), **Price**, **Place** (distribution), **Promotion** (advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, publicity). Services add People, Process, Physical evidence (7Ps).
**Segmentation:** dividing the market by geography, demographics (age, income), psychographics, behaviour. **Targeting** and **positioning** follow.

steps.title: Solved example

steps.title: Common mistake

scenes.text: A home baker wants 25% profit over cost.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: **Cost-plus price = cost per unit × (1 + markup%)**. **Margin% on price** = (price − cost) ÷ price × 100. Competitor and value-based pricing also matter. Discounts reduce price: sale price = marked price × (1 − discount%).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Cost ₹400 per cake, 25% markup → 400 × 1.25 = **₹500**. Margin on price = 100 ÷ 500 = **20%**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Marked price ₹500, 10% discount → 500 × 0.9 = **₹450**; profit = 450 − 400 = **₹50** (still above cost).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Confusing markup on cost (25%) with margin on price (20%).

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Internal growth:** expansion (more capacity or outlets), market penetration, new products, new markets.
- **Diversification:** related or unrelated products.
- **External growth:** merger, acquisition, joint venture, **franchising** (franchisee pays fee and royalty for brand and system).
- Risks: cash strain, loss of quality, management overload. Growth should follow demand and capacity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Revenue last year ₹12 lakh, this year ₹15 lakh. Growth = (15 − 12) ÷ 12 × 100 = **25%**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Growing too fast without cash flow; many firms fail from overtrading.

In India, companies meeting size thresholds must spend 2% of average net profit on CSR (Companies Act 2013) — small start-ups can still act voluntarily (waste reduction, local hiring).

steps.title: Method

steps.title: Solved example

school-c11-fineart.description: Original study notes on early Indian art for Class 11 Fine Art: prehistoric rock paintings, Indus Valley arts, Mauryan art and early Buddhist art, with timelines, comparisons and exam-style questions.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Prehistoric Rock Paintings
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

outcomes: Locate major prehistoric painting sites

scenes.text: A trekker enters a rock shelter in the Vindhya hills and sees red figures of bison and dancers on the wall.
Thousands of years ago, people painted these to record their world.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
India has numerous rock-art sites in rock shelters. **Bhimbetka** (near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh) is the most famous: hundreds of shelters with paintings, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2003). Other regions: Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh), Kaimur range, Raisen, Hoshangabad (Adamgarh), Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh (e.g. Kupgal, Piklihal), Odisha and Uttarakhand (Lakhu Udyar).
Paintings span many periods from the Upper Palaeolithic through Mesolithic to the historic era, so different layers show different styles.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Why do paintings at a single shelter look different? Because people painted over many thousands of years; older figures may lie beneath newer ones (superimposition) and help scholars establish a sequence.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying all rock paintings in India are of one period; they range widely, and dating is based on style, superimposition and associated finds.

scenes.text: A craftsperson grinds red stone into powder and mixes it with a binder.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Colours:** red (haematite/geru), white (limestone or kaolin), yellow ochre, green and black in some sites; red and white are most common at Bhimbetka.
- **Binders and tools:** natural binders such as plant gum or animal fat (reported by scholars), brushes of chewed twigs or fibres, fingers.
- **Themes:** hunting, animals (bison, deer, elephants, boars), dancing, community scenes, riders, masks, honey collecting; geometric and abstract signs.
- **Style:** early figures often large and naturalistic; later ones smaller, stylised and with action.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: What do hunting scenes tell us? They show weapons (bows, spears), group hunting, relations with animals and probably ritual importance; they hint at an economy based on hunting and gathering.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Mention colour, theme and style in every description answer.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: Rock art is a primary source for the lives, beliefs and environment of early people before writing. Threats: weathering, vandalism, graffiti, quarrying, careless tourism. Preservation: documentation (photography, 3D scanning), site guards, no touching, community involvement.

steps.title: Respect
steps.body: Do not touch or draw on heritage walls; report damage to the site authority.

scenes.text: A merchant presses a small stone seal into clay to mark a bundle of goods.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
The Indus (Harappan) civilisation flourished roughly 2600–1900 BCE (mature phase), with sites like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa (now in Pakistan), Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi (India).
- **Seals:** mostly square, made of **steatite**, with animals (unicorn bull, bull, elephant, tiger), deities and a script that is **still undeciphered**.
- **Sculpture:** the **Priest-king** bust (steatite) from Mohenjo-daro, with trefoil-patterned shawl; torso figures from Harappa.
- Art was small-scale, precise and linked with trade and administration.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Why are seals important for historians? They show trade (found at distant sites, including Mesopotamia), religion (animals/deities) and writing (undeciphered) — three kinds of evidence from one object.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming the Indus script has been deciphered; it has not.
- Calling the 'Priest-king' a confirmed priest or king; the name is a convention.

activity.prompt: Match object and material/place

scenes.text: A small bronze girl stands with a hand on her hip, wearing bangles up one arm.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Bronze (copper + tin) casting** by **lost-wax (cire perdue)**: make a wax model → coat with clay → heat to melt wax out → pour molten metal into the hollow → break the mould. The **Dancing Girl** (about 10.5 cm tall, Mohenjo-daro) is the best-known example; also bronze bullock cart and animals.
- **Terracotta:** mother-goddess figurines, toy carts, whistles, animals.
- **Pottery:** wheel-made, red with black painted designs (pipal leaves, fish scale, intersecting circles); painted jars and dishes.
- **Beads and ornaments** of carnelian, gold, faience; etched carnelian beads.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Order lost-wax steps: 1 wax model, 2 clay coating, 3 heating to remove wax, 4 pouring metal, 5 breaking the mould. This method is still used by artists today.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Placing 'pouring metal' before the wax is melted out.

The art is **utilitarian and refined**: seals for trade, pottery for use, small figurines for ritual. No large temples or palaces are clearly identified; sculpture is small-scale compared with later Mauryan art.

lessons.title: Ashoka's pillars and the Lion Capital

scenes.text: Ashoka's edicts were inscribed on tall pillars across the empire, topped by animals.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
The Mauryan empire (c. 321–185 BCE) saw large-scale **court art** under Chandragupta and especially **Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE)**.
- **Pillars:** monolithic, made of Chunar sandstone, highly polished (**Mauryan polish**), with a shaft, a lotus capital and an animal (lion, bull, elephant, horse).
- **Sarnath Lion Capital:** four lions back to back on an **abacus** with a wheel (*dharmachakra*) and four animals (elephant, bull, horse, lion) separated by wheels, over an inverted lotus. A modified version is **India's national emblem** (adopted 1950), with the motto *Satyameva Jayate*.
- Inscribed edicts in Brahmi (and Kharoshthi, Greek, Aramaic in the north-west).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Why did Ashoka use pillars? To publish his dhamma policy and edicts widely, and the pillars' height and polish projected imperial authority and Buddhist symbolism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the national emblem shows four lions fully visible; only three are visible.
- Confusing Ashoka's pillar with the later Gupta Iron Pillar.

statements.s: Mauryan pillars were polished sandstone
Only three lions are visible on the national emblem
Ashoka's edicts were in English

lessons.title: Court vs popular art; Yakshi and caves

scenes.text: One sculptor works for the emperor; another makes clay figures sold at a village fair.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Court art:** pillars, palace at Pataliputra, stupas.
- **Popular art:** Yaksha and Yakshi figures, terracotta, local shrines.
- **Didarganj Yakshi** (Patna): polished sandstone, a standing female figure with a chauri (fly-whisk), full of grace, rounded form and fine jewellery.
- **Rock-cut caves:** **Barabar and Nagarjuni hills** (Bihar), cut for Ajivika monks, with the polished interior walls; **Lomas Rishi cave** with an arched entrance imitating wood.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Classify: Lion capital → court art; Yakshi → popular tradition in sculpture (carved in polished stone); terracotta toys → popular art.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Court art served the state religion and empire; popular art arose in people's daily and local worship.

outcomes: Describe the parts of a stupa
Compare Gandhara and Mathura sculpture
Explain Sanchi's gateways
Describe Ajanta's paintings and caves

scenes.text: Pilgrims walk clockwise around a great dome, reading stories carved on gateways.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
A **stupa** is a solid dome (anda) built over relics, with a **harmika** (railing on top), **chhatra** (umbrella), **vedika** (railing), **pradakshina patha** (circumambulation path) and **toranas** (gateways).
**Sanchi Great Stupa** (Madhya Pradesh), begun under Ashoka and enlarged later; the four carved gateways (c. 1st century BCE–CE) show **Jataka tales** and events from the Buddha's life using **symbols** (wheel, footprints, empty throne, bodhi tree) rather than a human figure. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1989).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Why symbols? In early Buddhist art the Buddha was shown aniconically, through the bodhi tree for enlightenment, the wheel for the first sermon, and a stupa for his death (parinirvana).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying the Sanchi gateways show the Buddha in human form; that came later with Gandhara and Mathura.

activity.prompt: Match symbol to meaning

scenes.text: One Buddha has wavy hair and heavy robes like a Greek statue; another has a plain, smiling face and light robes.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
| Feature | Gandhara | Mathura |
| Region | North-west (Taxila, Peshawar) | Mathura, Uttar Pradesh |
| Influence | Greco-Roman | Indigenous Indian |
| Material | Grey schist/stucco | Spotted red sandstone |
| Look | Wavy hair, heavy drapery, muscular | Smooth, light robes, smiling |
Both flourished under the **Kushanas** (c. 1st–3rd century CE) and first showed the Buddha in human form.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Identify a statue of red sandstone with a round, smiling face and an ushnisha: Mathura school.

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: Gandhara = Greek-style grey; Mathura = Made in India, red.

activity.prompt: School

scenes.text: Lamplight reveals a bodhisattva painted with a gentle tilt of the head on a cave wall in Maharashtra.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body:
**Ajanta** (near Aurangabad, Maharashtra): about 30 rock-cut Buddhist caves cut into a horseshoe-shaped gorge between roughly the 2nd century BCE and 5th–6th century CE; **chaityas** (prayer halls with a stupa) and **viharas** (monasteries). Paintings in tempera on prepared plaster show Jataka tales and Buddha's life, with delicate lines, rich colours and emotional expression; famous **Padmapani** and **Vajrapani** in Cave 1. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983).
Painting steps: rough clay-and-fibre plaster → fine lime-plaster → outline sketch → colour application → burnishing.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Differentiate chaitya and vihara. Chaitya: hall for worship with a stupa at the end. Vihara: monastery with cells around a hall for monks' living.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling Ajanta paintings 'frescoes' strictly; they are mainly tempera on dry plaster (scholars often use the word mural).

Burnish the surface

school-c11-geography.title: Class 11 Geography · Fundamentals of Physical Geography
school-c11-geography.description: Chapter courses for Class 11 physical geography: geography as a discipline, the earth's origin, its interior, drifting continents and plates, and the atmosphere — with diagrams described in words, numericals and map practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Geography as a Discipline
courses.summary: What geography studies, why it is an integrating discipline, its physical and human branches, the systematic and regional approaches, and the links with other sciences.
outcomes: Learners can define geography and its core questions (what, where, why)
Learners can distinguish systematic and regional approaches
Learners can list branches of physical and human geography
Learners can explain geography's links with other disciplines
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

story.title: Why does Cherrapunji get so much rain?

scenes.text: Asha visits Meghalaya and notices clouds piling up against the hills.
Her question — why here? — is a geographer's question.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Geography studies the **earth as the home of humans**: the **spatial distribution** of physical and human phenomena and their **interrelationships**. Core questions: **What** (phenomena), **Where** (location/distribution), and **Why** (causal explanation). The word was first used by the Greek scholar **Eratosthenes** (276–194 BCE): *geo* (earth) + *graphos* (description).

steps.title: Integrating discipline
steps.body: Geography is a discipline of **synthesis**: it borrows from and contributes to physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, history. Every phenomenon varies over **space** and **time**. Nature and humans interact — e.g. technology raises human freedom from nature ('naturalisation of humans' → 'humanisation of nature').

steps.title: Solved: what, where, why
steps.body: Phenomenon: heavy rainfall. **What**: 11,000+ mm per year. **Where**: southern slopes of Meghalaya plateau. **Why**: moist south-west monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal are forced up by the funnel-shaped hills, cool and condense (orographic rain).

steps.title: Solved: environmental determinism vs possibilism
steps.body: Determinism: nature controls human life. Possibilism: humans choose among possibilities offered by nature using technology. Example: farmers in deserts using drip irrigation illustrate possibilism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Geography is not just 'maps and capitals' — it explains **why** distributions exist.

statements.s: Eratosthenes first used the word 'geography'.
Geography studies only physical features.
Space and time are central to geographical study.
Possibilism holds that nature fully controls human activity.

quiz.q: The term geography was first used by:
The 'why' question in geography deals with:
Geography is called a discipline of:

scenes.text: One student studies climate across all of India.
Another studies everything about the Western Ghats region.

steps.title: Two approaches
steps.body:
- **Systematic** approach (Alexander von **Humboldt**, German geographer): a phenomenon (e.g. climate) studied worldwide, then regions identified.
- **Regional** approach (Carl **Ritter**, Humboldt's contemporary): the world divided into regions, and all phenomena in a region studied together.
This led to the **dualism** debate — physical vs human, systematic vs regional.

steps.title: Branches
steps.body:
**Physical geography**: geomorphology (landforms), climatology, hydrology, soil geography, biogeography.
**Human geography**: social/cultural, population & settlement, economic, historical, political.
**Regional**: regional studies, regional planning, regional development.
Plus **cartography**, quantitative techniques, field survey, GIS.

steps.title: Solved: classify a study
steps.body: 'Distribution of monsoon rainfall in India' → systematic (climatology). 'Profile of the Chhotanagpur plateau region' → regional.

steps.title: Solved: physical geography's importance
steps.body: It explains landforms, climate, soils, water and vegetation — the resource base. Understanding it helps in disaster management (floods, landslides) and land use planning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Humboldt = systematic; Ritter = regional. Don't swap them.

activity.prompt: Physical or human geography branch?

quiz.q: Which is a branch of human geography?

scenes.text: Your school's geography club receives project proposals.
You must classify each one.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: For each proposal: identify the phenomenon → is it one theme worldwide (systematic) or one region in full (regional)? → which branch?

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Short answers: define + one example. Long: approaches, branches, links with sciences in a table.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Listing branches without classifying them as physical/human.

activity.prompt: Match the project to the branch

Assertion: Geography is integrating. Reason: It draws on natural and social sciences.
options: Both true; R doesn't explain A

courses.title: Ch 2 · The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
courses.summary: From early theories (nebular, planetesimal) to the Big Bang; star and planet formation; terrestrial vs Jovian planets; the Moon; the evolution of the lithosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere; and the origin of life.
outcomes: Learners can compare early and modern theories of origin
Learners can explain the formation of stars and planets
Learners can distinguish inner and outer planets
Learners can describe the stages in the evolution of the atmosphere
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Early theories and the Big Bang

scenes.text: Ravi marks dots on a balloon and inflates it — the dots move apart.
His teacher says galaxies behave the same way: the universe is expanding.

steps.title: Early theories
steps.body:
- **Nebular hypothesis**: Immanuel **Kant** (philosopher), revised by mathematician **Laplace** (1796) — planets formed from a cloud of material around a slowly rotating young sun.
- **Binary/companion star theories** and the **planetesimal hypothesis** by **Chamberlain and Moulton** (1900): a wandering star pulled material from the sun that condensed into planets.
- Later revised nebular ideas: **Otto Schmidt** and **Carl Weizsacker** (1950) — sun surrounded by a solar nebula of hydrogen, helium and dust; friction and collisions formed a disk and planets by accretion.

steps.title: Big Bang theory
steps.body: Also called the **expanding universe hypothesis**. **Edwin Hubble** (1920) showed galaxies are moving apart. Stages: 1) All matter in a 'tiny ball' (singular atom) of incredible density; 2) it exploded about **13.7 billion years** ago, expanding ever since; within fractions of a second, rapid expansion; 3) about 3 lakh years later, temperature fell to about 4,500 K, giving rise to atomic matter, and the universe became transparent.

steps.title: Solved: balloon analogy
steps.body: Points on a balloon move apart as it inflates — but the points themselves (galaxies) don't expand; the **space between them** does. Limitation: the balloon is a 2-D surface model of 3-D space.

steps.title: Solved: steady state
steps.body: Hoyle's **steady state** theory proposed the universe looks roughly the same at all times. Evidence of expansion and cosmic background favours the Big Bang today.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Big Bang was not an explosion **in** space but an expansion **of** space.

activity.prompt: Order these ideas by when they were proposed

events.text: Schmidt and Weizsacker: revised nebular hypothesis

quiz.q: Steady state theory was proposed by:

scenes.text: At Hanle, students see the Milky Way stretching across the sky.
They ask: why are Jupiter and Saturn so big and gassy, while Earth is rocky?

steps.title: Star formation
steps.body: Uneven distribution of matter → denser areas → **galaxies**. A galaxy starts as huge clouds of hydrogen gas (**nebula**); localised clumps grow by gravity into **stars**. The first galaxies formed within roughly the first billion years after the Big Bang; our **Milky Way** is about 100,000 light years across.

steps.title: Planet formation (stages)
steps.body: 1) Stars are localised lumps within a nebula; a gas cloud core forms with a disk of gas and dust around it. 2) The gas cloud condenses; matter around the core forms small rounded objects (**planetesimals**) by cohesion. 3) Planetesimals collide and gravity builds **planets**.

steps.title: Inner vs outer planets
steps.body: **Terrestrial (inner)**: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — rocky, dense, small. **Jovian/gas giants (outer)**: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — large, gaseous. Why different: inner planets formed close to the star where it was too hot for gases to condense; solar wind blew gases away; smaller size meant weaker gravity to hold gas.

steps.title: The Moon
steps.body: Earlier idea: Earth and Moon formed one rapidly rotating body that split (Sir George Darwin, 1838). Now accepted: a **giant impact** — a body about the size of Mars or larger collided with the early Earth, blasting out material that formed the Moon, about **4.44 billion years** ago.

steps.title: Solved: three reasons for rocky inner planets
steps.body: 1) High temperature near the sun prevented gas condensation. 2) Strong solar wind removed gases. 3) Lower gravity of small planets could not retain escaping gases.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pluto is no longer counted among the eight planets (reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006).

activity.prompt: Explore the solar system. Tap the terrestrial planets, then a gas giant.

quiz.q: Inner planets are rocky partly because:
options: They are farther from the sun

quiz.q: The Moon is thought to have formed by:

options: Small bodies that combine into planets

lessons.title: Evolution of the earth and life

story.title: From fire ball to blue planet

scenes.text: Early Earth was barren, rocky and hot, with a thin atmosphere of hydrogen and helium.
Over hundreds of millions of years, oceans formed and life appeared.

steps.title: Layered earth
steps.body: Earth was initially volatile. As density increased, heavier materials (iron) sank to the centre and lighter ones rose — **differentiation** — forming crust, mantle, outer core, inner core. A giant impact formed the Moon; heat again melted the earth.

steps.title: Atmosphere in three stages
steps.body:
1) **Loss of primordial atmosphere** (hydrogen, helium) stripped by solar winds.
2) Hot interior released gases and water vapour — **degassing**; volcanic eruptions added water vapour, nitrogen, CO₂, methane, ammonia, little free oxygen.
3) **Photosynthesis** by life modified the composition; oceans formed ~4 billion years ago as vapour condensed and rain fell; life appeared around 3.8 billion years ago; photosynthesis evolved about 2.5–3 billion years ago and oceans filled with oxygen, which then flooded the atmosphere about 2 billion years ago.

steps.title: Solved: degassing
steps.body: **Q:** What is degassing? **A:** The release of gases from the earth's hot interior during its cooling and through volcanic activity — it built the second atmosphere.

steps.title: Solved: time arithmetic
steps.body: Earth formed ~4.6 bya; life ~3.8 bya → about **0.8 billion (800 million) years** passed before life appeared.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Early atmosphere had very little free oxygen; oxygen came from photosynthesis.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Interior of the Earth
courses.summary: Direct and indirect sources of knowledge about the interior, earthquakes and seismic waves, shadow zones, crust–mantle–core structure, volcanoes and volcanic landforms.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish direct and indirect sources
Learners can explain P, S and surface waves and shadow zones
Learners can describe crust, mantle and core with depths
Learners can classify volcanoes and intrusive landforms
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A seismograph in Dehradun records a squiggle seconds before the shaking is felt.
Seismologists use such records worldwide to 'see' inside the earth.

steps.title: Direct and indirect sources
steps.body:
**Direct**: mining (South African gold mines ~3–4 km deep), deep drilling (Kola Superdeep, ~12 km, Arctic; Deep Ocean Drilling Project), volcanic eruptions (magma).
**Indirect**: temperature/pressure/density increase with depth, **meteors**, **gravitation** anomalies, **magnetic** surveys, and most importantly **seismic activity**.

steps.title: Earthquakes
steps.body: Release of energy along a **fault** generates waves. **Focus/hypocentre**: point of origin below the surface. **Epicentre**: point on the surface directly above. Types: tectonic (most common), volcanic, collapse (mining areas), explosion, reservoir-induced. Measured on the **Richter scale** (magnitude, 0–10) and **Mercalli scale** (intensity/damage, 1–12).

steps.title: Solved: magnitude comparison
steps.body: Richter is logarithmic: each whole number = **10 times** more ground amplitude (about 32 times more energy). A magnitude 7 vs 5 → 10² = **100 times** larger amplitude.

steps.title: Solved: effects of earthquakes
steps.body: Ground shaking, differential ground settlement, land and mud slides, soil liquefaction, ground lurching, avalanches, ground displacement, floods from dam failures, fires, structural collapse, tsunamis (if under sea).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Epicentre is on the surface; focus is below. Richter = magnitude, Mercalli = intensity.

activity.prompt: How many times greater is the ground amplitude of a magnitude 8 earthquake than a magnitude 5?

quiz.q: Point inside the earth where an earthquake originates:

scenes.text: Stations on the far side of the earth from a quake record P-waves but no S-waves.
This absence revealed that the outer core is liquid.

steps.title: Body and surface waves
steps.body:
- **P-waves** (primary): fastest, first to arrive; **longitudinal** (vibrate parallel to direction); travel through solids, liquids and gases.
- **S-waves** (secondary): slower; **transverse** (vibrate perpendicular); travel **only through solids**.
- **Surface waves**: generated when body waves interact with surface rocks; last to arrive; most destructive.

steps.title: Shadow zones (diagram in words)
steps.body: Imagine the earth as a circle with the focus at the top. Measuring angles from the epicentre: seismographs within **105°** record both P and S. Beyond **145°** only P-waves arrive. Between **105° and 145°** neither is recorded — the **P-wave shadow zone** (a belt around the earth). For S-waves, the shadow is everything beyond **105°** — much larger (over 40% of the earth's surface). Cause: liquid outer core blocks S; P-waves are refracted by the core.

steps.title: Solved: shadow zone reasoning
steps.body: **Q:** Why do S-waves not reach beyond 105°? **A:** 1) S-waves cannot travel through liquids. 2) The outer core is liquid. 3) So any path passing through the outer core loses S-waves → large S shadow zone.

steps.title: Solved: arrival time
steps.body: If P travels at 8 km/s and S at 4.5 km/s over 720 km: P = 90 s, S = 160 s → S arrives **70 s** after P. The lag lets seismologists estimate distance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: P-waves are not blocked by liquid — they slow and refract.

statements.s: P-waves can travel through liquids.
S-waves are longitudinal.
The P-wave shadow zone lies between 105° and 145°.
Surface waves arrive first.
The S-wave shadow zone is larger than the P-wave shadow zone.

quiz.q: P at 8 km/s, S at 4 km/s over 800 km — lag?

scenes.text: Imagine an elevator going 6,371 km down.
Temperature and pressure rise; at 2,900 km the rock turns into liquid metal.

steps.title: Crust
steps.body: Outermost solid, brittle layer. **Oceanic crust** ~5 km thick; **continental** ~30 km on average, up to ~70 km under the **Himalaya**. Density about **3 g/cm³**; oceanic crust made largely of basalt.

steps.title: Mantle
steps.body: From the Moho discontinuity to **2,900 km**. Upper part is the **asthenosphere** (up to ~400 km) — weak, source of magma. Crust + uppermost mantle = **lithosphere** (10–200 km). Mantle density > 3.4 g/cm³, solid overall.

steps.title: Core
steps.body: From **2,900 km to 6,371 km** (centre). **Outer core**: liquid; **inner core**: solid. Density ~5 g/cm³ at mantle-core boundary rising to ~13 g/cm³ at centre. Made of nickel and iron — 'barysphere' / **nife**.

steps.title: Solved: thicknesses
steps.body: Mantle thickness ≈ 2,900 − 30 = **2,870 km** (continental). Core thickness = 6,371 − 2,900 = **3,471 km**.

steps.title: Solved: why asthenosphere matters
steps.body: It is partially molten and weak, allowing plates above to move, and is the main source of magma for volcanoes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Lithosphere ≠ crust; it includes the upper mantle.

activity.prompt: Explore the earth's layers. Tap each layer and compare depth and state.

scenes.text: In the Andaman Sea, Barren Island — India's only active volcano — puffs smoke.
On the Deccan plateau, layers of black basalt record ancient eruptions.

steps.title: Types of volcanoes
steps.body:
- **Shield**: largest; mostly basalt, very fluid lava; gentle slopes (Hawaiian).
- **Composite**: cooler, viscous lava; explosive; layers of lava and ash.
- **Caldera**: most explosive; collapse after eruption.
- **Flood basalt provinces**: highly fluid lava over large areas — e.g. **Deccan Traps**.
- **Mid-ocean ridge volcanoes**: e.g. along the mid-Atlantic ridge.

steps.title: Intrusive landforms (diagram in words)
steps.body:
Magma cooling inside the crust forms:
- **Batholith**: huge dome-shaped granite body deep in the crust.
- **Laccolith**: dome with a level base, connected by a pipe below (e.g. Karnataka granite domes).
- **Lapolith**: saucer shape, concave up.
- **Phacolith**: wavy mass at the base of synclines/top of anticlines.
- **Sill**: horizontal sheet (thin = sheet).
- **Dyke**: vertical wall-like body, common in western Maharashtra (feeders for Deccan Traps).

steps.title: Solved: shield vs composite
steps.body: Shield: fluid basalt, low silica, gentle slope, mild eruptions. Composite: viscous, high silica, steep cone, explosive. Viscosity explains the difference.

steps.title: Solved: identify
steps.body: A vertical wall of volcanic rock cutting across layers → **dyke**. A horizontal sheet parallel to layers → **sill**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Lava = magma that reaches the surface. Batholith is intrusive (formed inside), not on the surface.

activity.prompt: Match the landform
pairs: Large granite body deep in crust
Dome with level base and pipe below

scenes.text: Three stations record P–S lags after a quake.
You estimate the distance and identify safety steps.

steps.title: Distance from lag
steps.body: Distance d satisfies d/vS − d/vP = lag. With vP = 8 km/s and vS = 4.5 km/s: d = lag × (8 × 4.5)/(8 − 4.5) ≈ lag × 10.29 km.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Drop, cover, hold on. Stay away from windows. After shaking, move to open ground; beware of aftershocks. Emergency: 112.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the formula uses the difference of travel times.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Distribution of Oceans and Continents
courses.summary: Wegener's continental drift and its evidence, post-drift studies (convection currents, ocean-floor mapping, sea-floor spreading), plate tectonics and plate boundaries, rates of movement, and the movement of the Indian plate.
outcomes: Learners can state continental drift and evaluate its evidence
Learners can explain sea-floor spreading
Learners can classify plate boundaries with examples
Learners can narrate the northward journey of the Indian plate
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Neha notices that Brazil's bulge seems to fit into West Africa's coast.
In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener turned this into a theory.

steps.title: Wegener's theory (1912)
steps.body: All continents formed a single mass, **Pangaea**, surrounded by a mega-ocean, **Panthalassa**. About **200 million years** ago Pangaea began to split into **Laurasia** (north) and **Gondwanaland** (south), which further broke into modern continents.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body:
- **Jig-saw fit**: Bullard (1964) computer fit at the 1,000-fathom line.
- **Rocks of the same age** across oceans: 2,000-million-year-old belts of Brazil and West Africa match.
- **Tillite** (glacial deposits): Gondwana sediments in India match those in Africa, Falkland, Madagascar, Antarctica, Australia.
- **Placer gold** in Ghana with no source rock — source in Brazil.
- **Fossils**: *Mesosaurus* in South Africa and Brazil (Iraver formation); lemurs in India, Madagascar, Africa (idea of 'Lemuria').

steps.title: Forces proposed
steps.body: **Pole-fleeing force** (earth's rotation) and **tidal force** (sun and moon). Most scholars found these far too weak — a key weakness.

steps.title: Solved: why tillite is strong evidence
steps.body: Tillite forms from glaciers. Finding identical glacial deposits in now-tropical India and Africa means these lands were once together near a pole.

steps.title: Solved: evaluate
steps.body: Strengths: multiple independent evidence lines. Weakness: no convincing mechanism — later solved by convection currents and sea-floor spreading.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Wegener was a meteorologist, and drift was proposed in **1912**, not 1960s (that is plate tectonics).

activity.prompt: Match evidence to its example
pairs: Mesosaurus in South Africa and Brazil

scenes.text: After World War II, ships sonar-map the ocean floor and find a mountain chain in mid-Atlantic.
Rocks show stripes of reversed magnetism, mirrored on both sides.

steps.title: Convection currents
steps.body: **Arthur Holmes** (1930s) proposed convection currents in the mantle driven by radioactive heat and differences in temperature — a possible mechanism for drift.

steps.title: Ocean floor features
steps.body:
- **Continental margins**: shelf, slope, rise, deep-ocean trenches.
- **Abyssal plains**: flat, between margins and ridges.
- **Mid-oceanic ridges**: interconnected chain with a central rift; most volcanically active.

steps.title: Sea-floor spreading (Hess, 1961)
steps.body: Observations: rocks equidistant on either side of the ridge show same age and magnetism; rocks closer to the ridge are youngest; ocean crust is much younger than continental crust (no ocean floor older than ~200 million years); sediments thin near ridges; deep trenches have deep earthquakes. Hess: magma rises at ridges, creates new crust that spreads away; old crust sinks at trenches (**subduction**).

steps.title: Solved: why is ocean crust young?
steps.body: It is constantly created at ridges and destroyed at trenches — so it never gets very old (≤ ~200 Ma), unlike continental rocks up to ~3,200 Ma.

steps.title: Solved: spreading rate
steps.body: If rock 100 km from a ridge is 5 million years old: rate = 100 km / 5 Ma = 20 km/Ma = **2 cm/year** (1 km/Ma = 0.1 cm/yr).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Holmes = convection; Hess = sea-floor spreading. Don't swap them.

activity.prompt: A rock 150 km from a mid-ocean ridge is 10 million years old. Spreading rate on that side in cm/year?

lessons.title: Plate tectonics and the Indian plate

scenes.text: About 71 million years ago India sat far south, over a volcanic hotspot.
It moved north and collided with Asia, raising the Himalaya.

steps.title: Plates
steps.body: Plate tectonics (McKenzie and Parker 1967; Morgan 1968): the lithosphere is broken into rigid **plates** moving over the asthenosphere. **Seven major plates**: Antarctic, North American, South American, Pacific, India-Australia-New Zealand, Africa, Eurasia. Minor: Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji.

steps.title: Boundaries
steps.body:
- **Divergent** (constructive): plates move apart, new crust forms — mid-Atlantic ridge. Sites are **spreading sites**.
- **Convergent** (destructive): crust sinks — oceanic-continental, oceanic-oceanic, continental-continental. **Subduction zones**.
- **Transform** (conservative): plates slide past; crust neither created nor destroyed (transform faults).
Rates: Arctic Ridge slowest (< 2.5 cm/yr); **East Pacific Rise** fastest (> 15 cm/yr).

steps.title: Indian plate
steps.body: Boundaries: north — Himalaya (continent-continent convergence); east — Rakinyoma mountains of Myanmar to an arc along the Java trench; west — Kirthar mountains of Pakistan, along the Makran coast, joining the Red Sea rift; south-east/south — spreading site with Antarctic plate. About **225 Ma** India was an island off Australia; Tethys Sea separated it from Asia. About **200 Ma** Pangaea broke up. India moved north; **~71 Ma** over the **Réunion hotspot**, the **Deccan Traps** erupted (~60 Ma). Collision with Asia ~40–50 Ma raised the Himalaya; uplift continues.

steps.title: Solved: drift vs plate tectonics
steps.body: Drift: continents move through ocean floor; forces weak. Plate tectonics: lithospheric plates (continent + ocean) move together, driven by mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull.

steps.title: Solved: rate
steps.body: At 5 cm/yr, distance in 50 million years = 5 × 50,000,000 cm = 250,000,000 cm = **2,500 km**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Himalaya are a convergent (not divergent) boundary.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Composition and Structure of Atmosphere
courses.summary: Gases, water vapour and dust in the atmosphere; the layers from troposphere to exosphere with heights and temperature trends; elements of weather and climate.
outcomes: Learners can list atmospheric gases with proportions
Learners can explain the role of water vapour and dust
Learners can describe each atmospheric layer with heights
Learners can apply the lapse rate to compute temperature
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A biker gasps at 5,300 m in Ladakh.
Air still has ~21% oxygen — but its density is much lower.

steps.title: Gases
steps.body: Permanent gases by volume: **Nitrogen ~78.08%**, **Oxygen ~20.95%**, **Argon ~0.93%**, **Carbon dioxide ~0.04%** (rising), plus neon, helium, ozone, hydrogen, krypton, xenon, methane in traces. Up to about 120 km, gas proportions are uniform; density falls rapidly with height. Oxygen is negligible at 120 km; CO₂ and water vapour are found only up to ~90 km.

steps.title: Water vapour and dust
steps.body: **Water vapour**: variable — up to 4% in warm, wet tropics; less than 1% in cold, dry areas and deserts; decreases with height. It absorbs incoming and outgoing radiation, keeps the earth warm, and gives clouds and rain. **Dust particles**: sea salt, fine soil, smoke, ash, pollen; concentrated in subtropical and temperate regions due to dry winds; act as **hygroscopic nuclei** around which water condenses.

steps.title: Ozone and CO₂
steps.body: **CO₂** is transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation — the **greenhouse effect**. **Ozone** (10–50 km, mostly) filters ultraviolet radiation.

steps.title: Solved: percentage in a sample
steps.body: In 1,000 litres of dry air: N₂ ≈ 780.8 L, O₂ ≈ 209.5 L, Ar ≈ 9.3 L.

steps.title: Solved: why water vapour matters
steps.body: 1) Source of precipitation. 2) Absorbs heat, acts as a blanket. 3) Releases latent heat when it condenses, fuelling storms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Argon, not CO₂, is the third most abundant gas.

activity.prompt: How many litres of oxygen are in 500 litres of dry air (O₂ = 20.95%)? Round to one decimal.

scenes.text: A balloon launched from Chennai climbs through clouds; temperature falls steadily.
Above about 18 km the temperature stops falling — it has reached the tropopause.

steps.title: Troposphere
steps.body: Lowest layer: average height **13 km**; about **8 km** at poles and **18 km** at equator (thicker due to strong convection). All weather occurs here. Temperature falls about **1 °C per 165 m** (normal lapse rate ≈ 6.5 °C/km). **Tropopause**: boundary; about **−80 °C** over the equator and **−45 °C** over the poles.

steps.title: Stratosphere to exosphere
steps.body:
- **Stratosphere**: up to **50 km**; contains the **ozone layer**; temperature rises with height (ozone absorbs UV).
- **Mesosphere**: 50–80 km; temperature falls to about **−100 °C** at 80 km (mesopause).
- **Ionosphere** (thermosphere): 80–400 km; electrically charged particles (ions) reflect radio waves back to earth; temperature rises with height.
- **Exosphere**: uppermost; very thin; gradually merges with space.

steps.title: Solved: why thicker at equator
steps.body: Strong heating at the equator causes powerful convection currents that carry heat to greater heights, raising the tropopause.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Temperature does **not** fall in every layer: it rises in the stratosphere and thermosphere.

bands.text: Troposphere (avg 13 km; 8 km poles, 18 km equator) — weather, temperature falls with height
Stratosphere — ozone layer, temperature rises with height

quiz.q: Radio waves are reflected by the:

scenes.text: Commercial jets cruise at 10–12 km, near the top of the troposphere in mid-latitudes.
You must brief passengers on outside conditions.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: Surface 35 °C at Delhi; cruise 11 km. Using 6.5 °C/km: 35 − 71.5 = **−36.5 °C**.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Draw a layered diagram: heights on the y-axis, temperature line zig-zagging (falls, rises, falls, rises).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using 165 m and 6.5 °C/km in the same calculation inconsistently — pick one and round sensibly.

scenes.text: यमुना के पुल पर आधी रात को गाड़ियों की लंबी क़तार।
नए दारोगा वंशीधर ने रोका — इनमें नमक है, जो बिना कर के ले जाया जा रहा है!
पंडित अलोपीदीन मुस्कराए — 'हम आपको ख़ुश कर देंगे…' पर वंशीधर नहीं झुके।

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **प्रेमचंद** (1880–1936) ने ग्रामीण भारत, किसान, स्त्री और भ्रष्टाचार पर यथार्थवादी कहानियाँ लिखीं। 'नमक का दारोगा' आदर्शोन्मुख यथार्थवाद का उदाहरण है।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
नमक का नया विभाग बना था, जिसमें ऊपरी आमदनी (रिश्वत) बहुत थी। **मुंशी वंशीधर** को पिता ने सीख दी — 'मासिक वेतन पूर्णमासी का चाँद है, ऊपरी आय बहता स्रोत।' पर वंशीधर ईमानदार निकले। एक रात उन्होंने इलाक़े के सबसे प्रतिष्ठित ज़मींदार **पंडित अलोपीदीन** की नमक से भरी गाड़ियाँ पकड़ीं। अलोपीदीन ने एक हज़ार से चालीस हज़ार तक की रिश्वत की पेशकश की, पर वंशीधर ने उन्हें **गिरफ़्तार** कर लिया।

अदालत में धन और प्रभाव के बल पर अलोपीदीन **बरी** हो गए; वंशीधर की 'उद्दंडता' पर टिप्पणी हुई और उन्हें **नौकरी से निकाल** दिया गया। घर पर पिता ने कोसा। कुछ दिनों बाद अलोपीदीन स्वयं वंशीधर के घर आए और अपनी सारी जायदाद का **स्थायी मैनेजर** बनाने का प्रस्ताव दिया — क्योंकि उन्हें ऐसा ही ईमानदार, धर्मनिष्ठ व्यक्ति चाहिए था। वंशीधर ने भावुक होकर स्वीकार किया।

steps.body:

steps.title: शब्द-अर्थ
steps.body:
- **दारोगा** — विभाग का निरीक्षक अधिकारी
- **ऊपरी आय** — रिश्वत/वेतन के अतिरिक्त कमाई
- **उद्दंडता** — अक्खड़पन, धृष्टता
- **बरी** — आरोप से मुक्त
- **मुख्तार** — कानूनी प्रतिनिधि
- **धर्मनिष्ठ** — धर्म/कर्तव्य में दृढ़
- **अलौकिक** — असाधारण

steps.title: वाक्य-प्रयोग
steps.body:
- अदालत ने अलोपीदीन को **बरी** कर दिया।
- वंशीधर **धर्मनिष्ठ** अधिकारी थे।

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- वंशीधर अंत में हारते नहीं — नैतिक विजय उन्हीं की है।
- अलोपीदीन ने बदला लेने नहीं, सम्मान देने के लिए वंशीधर को बुलाया।
- 'दारोगा' यहाँ पुलिस का नहीं, **नमक विभाग** का अधिकारी है।

scenes.text: अध्यापिका ने पूछा — रचनाकार हमसे क्या कहना चाहता है?
आरव ने पाठ की एक बात को आज के जीवन से जोड़ा।

steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: कहानी में दो संसार हैं — अलोपीदीन का, जहाँ 'लक्ष्मी' (धन) सब ख़रीद सकती है, और वंशीधर का, जहाँ धर्म अडिग है। अदालत का दृश्य दिखाता है कि वकील, गवाह, जज — सब धन से प्रभावित थे। पर अलोपीदीन धनी होते हुए भी गुणों के पारखी हैं; उन्हें एहसास होता है कि जो व्यक्ति चालीस हज़ार ठुकरा दे, वही उनकी संपत्ति का सच्चा रक्षक हो सकता है। यह प्रेमचंद का आदर्शवाद है — ईमानदारी अंततः पुरस्कृत होती है।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: आज भी ईमानदार अधिकारियों पर दबाव, ट्रांसफ़र या निलंबन की ख़बरें आती हैं। भ्रष्टाचार की शिकायत के लिए केंद्रीय सतर्कता आयोग जैसी संस्थाएँ हैं। कंपनियाँ भी ईमानदार कर्मचारियों को सबसे ज़्यादा महत्त्व देती हैं।

steps.title: केंद्रीय भाव / संदेश
steps.body: ईमानदारी की राह कठिन है, पर अंततः सम्मान और विश्वास वही दिलाती है।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** कहानी का कौन-सा पात्र आपको सर्वाधिक प्रभावित करता है और क्यों?
**उत्तर:** वंशीधर — क्योंकि गरीबी, पिता के दबाव और चालीस हज़ार की रिश्वत के बावजूद वे ईमानदार रहे। उन्होंने नौकरी खो दी पर धर्म नहीं छोड़ा।

**प्रश्न:** 'नमक का दारोगा' कहानी में पंडित अलोपीदीन के व्यक्तित्व के कौन-से दो पहलू उभरकर आते हैं?
**उत्तर:** (1) धन के बल पर सब कुछ ख़रीदने वाला चतुर, प्रभावशाली ज़मींदार; (2) गुणों का पारखी, जो ईमानदारी का सम्मान कर वंशीधर को ऊँचा पद देता है।

steps.title: व्याकरण बिंदु
steps.body:
**मुहावरे (पाठ से)**: 'फूले न समाना' = बहुत ख़ुश होना; 'सन्नाटा छाना'; 'हाथ मलना' = पछताना; 'मुँह में कालिख लगना' = बदनामी।

**लोकोक्ति**: 'मासिक वेतन पूर्णमासी का चाँद है' — रूपक।

steps.title: उत्तर लिखने की युक्ति
steps.body:
- पहले प्रश्न का मुख्य शब्द पहचानें।

लेखिका पत्रकार की तरह सवाल पूछती हैं, मियाँ मज़े से — और कभी झुँझलाकर — जवाब देते हैं।

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **कृष्णा सोबती** (1925–2019) हिंदी की प्रमुख कथाकार। 'ज़िंदगीनामा' पर साहित्य अकादमी, 2017 में ज्ञानपीठ। 'मित्रो मरजानी', 'डार से बिछुड़ी' प्रसिद्ध। 'हम हशमत' में शब्दचित्र।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
लेखिका एक दोपहर **मटियामहल** के **गढ़ैया मोहल्ले** में एक अँधेरी दुकान पर पहुँचती हैं, जहाँ **मियाँ नसीरुद्दीन** बैठे हैं। वे स्वयं को **खानदानी नानबाई** बताते हैं, जो **छप्पन किस्म की रोटियाँ** बनाते हैं। लेखिका के प्रश्नों पर वे पहले अपने **पेशे की प्रतिष्ठा** बताते हैं — 'काम करने से आता है, किताबों से नहीं'; उन्होंने यह कला अपने **वालिद** (पिता) और **दादा** से सीखी, जैसे बच्चा पहले 'अलिफ़-बे' सीखता है।

वे बताते हैं कि उनके बुज़ुर्ग **बादशाह** के शाही बावर्चीख़ाने में काम कर चुके थे — पर कौन-से बादशाह, पूछने पर टाल जाते हैं। रोटियों के नाम पूछने पर गिनाते हैं — बाक़रख़ानी, शीरमाल, ताफ़तान, बेसनी, ख़मीरी, रूमाली, गाव, दीदा, गाज़ेबान, तुनकी… आख़िर में झुँझलाकर कहते हैं कि अब कारीगरी का सम्मान नहीं, लोग मशीनी चीज़ें पसंद करते हैं। वे कारीगरों (कुर्सी पर बैठे-बैठे) को काम पर लगाते हैं, उन्हें 'मज़दूरी' देने की बात पर भड़कते हैं।
