steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: लेखिका ने साक्षात्कार की शैली में एक व्यक्तित्व खड़ा किया है। मियाँ का गर्व केवल अहंकार नहीं — यह उस कारीगरी का स्वाभिमान है जो पीढ़ियों से चली आई। उनका कथन 'हमने भी यह इल्म सीखा, जैसे बच्चा अलिफ़-बे सीखता है' बताता है कि हुनर निरंतर अभ्यास से आता है। अंत की झुँझलाहट में बदलते समय के प्रति शिकायत है — मशीनों और बाज़ार ने पारंपरिक हुनर का मूल्य घटा दिया।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: आज 'हस्तशिल्प', 'आर्टिज़न ब्रेड', 'लोकल फ़ूड' फिर लोकप्रिय हो रहे हैं। किसी भी काम को सम्मान देना और कौशल (skill) को डिग्री जितना महत्त्व देना ज़रूरी है।

steps.title: केंद्रीय भाव / संदेश
steps.body: हर पेशे का सम्मान करें; कारीगरी अनुभव, अभ्यास और समर्पण से आती है।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** मियाँ नसीरुद्दीन को नानबाइयों का मसीहा क्यों कहा गया है?
**उत्तर:** वे खानदानी नानबाई हैं, छप्पन किस्म की रोटियाँ बनाने का दावा करते हैं, और नानबाई के पेशे को कला मानकर उसका सम्मान करते हैं; इसलिए उन्हें नानबाइयों का मसीहा कहा गया।

**प्रश्न:** लेखिका मियाँ नसीरुद्दीन के पास क्यों गई थीं?
**उत्तर:** वे उनके पेशे और खानदानी हुनर के बारे में जानना चाहती थीं — एक पत्रकार की तरह उनसे बातचीत करके उनका शब्दचित्र लिखने के लिए।

काशफूलों से भरे मैदान में शूटिंग शुरू हुई… और अगली बार तक जानवर सारे फूल खा गए!

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **सत्यजित राय** (1921–1992) विश्वप्रसिद्ध भारतीय फ़िल्मकार। 'पथेर पांचाली' (1955), 'चारुलता', 'शतरंज के खिलाड़ी' आदि। 1992 में मानद ऑस्कर और भारत रत्न। यह पाठ उनके बांग्ला संस्मरण का हिंदी अनुवाद है।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
'पथेर पांचाली' (विभूतिभूषण बंद्योपाध्याय के उपन्यास पर आधारित) की शूटिंग **ढाई साल** चली, क्योंकि लेखक के पास **पैसे** नहीं थे; पैसे जुटने पर ही शूटिंग होती। अपू की भूमिका के लिए छह साल का लड़का मिलना कठिन था; अख़बार में विज्ञापन दिया, अंततः पड़ोस का **सुबीर बनर्जी** मिला। इतने लंबे समय में बच्चों के बड़े होने का डर था।

एक दृश्य में अपू-दुर्गा **काशफूलों** से भरे मैदान से रेलगाड़ी देखने जाते हैं; आधी शूटिंग के बाद अगले हफ़्ते तक जानवर काशफूल खा गए, तो अगले साल शरद में फूल खिलने तक इंतज़ार करना पड़ा। रेलगाड़ी के धुएँ के लिए तीन ट्रेनें इस्तेमाल हुईं। कुत्ते **भूलो** की मृत्यु के बाद हमशक्ल कुत्ता लाया गया। मिठाईवाले **श्रीनिवास** का पात्र निभाने वाले व्यक्ति की मृत्यु हुई, तो उसी डील-डौल के दूसरे व्यक्ति को पीठ दिखाकर दृश्य पूरा किया गया। **बारिश** का दृश्य पैसे न होने से बरसात बीत जाने के बाद अक्टूबर में शरद में बारिश की प्रतीक्षा करके फ़िल्माया गया। गाँव के **सुबोध दा** शूटिंग वालों को शक की नज़र से देखते थे।

steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: यह पाठ सिखाता है कि रचनात्मक काम में समस्याएँ आती हैं, पर धैर्य और सूझ-बूझ से हल निकलते हैं। हर बाधा — पैसे, बच्चे का बढ़ना, कुत्ते की मृत्यु, कलाकार की मृत्यु, मौसम — का राय ने रचनात्मक समाधान निकाला। 'पीठ दिखाकर दृश्य पूरा करना' जैसी तरकीबें फ़िल्म-निर्माण की बारीकियाँ बताती हैं। अनुभवहीन टीम ने ढाई साल में विश्व सिनेमा की कालजयी फ़िल्म बनाई।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: आज लघु फ़िल्म या स्कूल प्रोजेक्ट बनाते समय भी बजट, मौसम और कलाकार की समस्याएँ आती हैं। राय का धैर्य और 'जुगाड़' सोच — कम संसाधनों में सर्वश्रेष्ठ — स्टार्टअप्स के लिए भी सीख है।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** 'पथेर पांचाली' फ़िल्म की शूटिंग का काम ढाई साल तक क्यों चला?
**उत्तर:** लेखक के पास पर्याप्त पैसे नहीं थे; पैसे जुटने पर ही शूटिंग होती, फिर रुक जाती। साथ ही कलाकारों, मौसम (काशफूल, बारिश) की समस्याएँ भी आईं।

**प्रश्न:** फ़िल्म में श्रीनिवास की क्या भूमिका थी और उनसे जुड़े बाकी दृश्यों को उनके गुज़र जाने के बाद किस प्रकार फ़िल्माया गया?
**उत्तर:** श्रीनिवास घूमने वाले मिठाईवाले थे। उनकी भूमिका निभाने वाले व्यक्ति की मृत्यु के बाद उसी कद-काठी के दूसरे व्यक्ति को लेकर उसकी पीठ कैमरे की ओर रखकर बाक़ी दृश्य फ़िल्माए गए।

steps.title: व्याकरण बिंदु
steps.body:

**प्रत्यय 'हीन'**: अनुभवहीन, गुणहीन, शक्तिहीन — अभाव बताता है।

**संधि**: स्थान + आपन्न = स्थानापन्न (दीर्घ संधि)।

- पाठ से एक घटना या पंक्ति का उदाहरण दें।
- छोटे प्रश्न में 3–4 वाक्य, बड़े प्रश्न में 6–7 वाक्य लिखें।

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **बालमुकुंद गुप्त** (1865–1907) भारतेंदु युग और द्विवेदी युग के बीच की कड़ी, पत्रकार और व्यंग्यकार। 'भारत मित्र' के संपादक। 'शिवशंभु के चिट्ठे' उनकी प्रसिद्ध व्यंग्य-रचना है।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
लेखक **शिवशंभु** के नाम से लॉर्ड **कर्ज़न** को संबोधित करते हैं। कर्ज़न दो बार वायसराय बने; दूसरी बार उन्हें इस्तीफ़ा देना पड़ा क्योंकि उनकी सिफ़ारिश पर एक सैनिक अफ़सर की नियुक्ति नहीं हुई — लेखक व्यंग्य करते हैं कि जिसके इशारे पर भारत नाचता था, उसकी एक बात भी इंग्लैंड ने नहीं मानी।

लेखक कहते हैं — विदाई का समय करुणा का होता है; भारत में तो **पशु-पक्षी** भी बिछुड़ते समय दुखी होते हैं (जैसे शिवशंभु की दो गायों का उदाहरण, और सीता के वनवास पर पशु-पक्षियों का दुख)। पर कर्ज़न ने अपने शासन में **प्रजा की भावनाओं** की उपेक्षा की: दिल्ली दरबार की शान-शौकत, **बंग-भंग** (1905), भारतीयों की बात न सुनना। उनके शासन में **नादिरशाह** से भी बुरा हाल हुआ — नादिरशाह ने भी कत्लेआम रोकने की प्रार्थना सुन ली थी, पर कर्ज़न ने आठ करोड़ लोगों की बंग-भंग न करने की प्रार्थना नहीं सुनी। लेखक पूछते हैं — आपने भारत को क्या दिया?

- बंग-भंग 1905 में हुआ, 1947 के विभाजन से न मिलाएँ।

steps.body: व्यंग्य की शक्ति इसकी विनम्र भाषा में है — लेखक 'माई लॉर्ड' कहकर आदर से बोलते हैं, पर हर बात तीखी है। वे भारतीय संस्कृति की संवेदनशीलता (विदाई में पशु-पक्षी भी रोते हैं) को कर्ज़न की संवेदनहीनता के सामने रखते हैं। नादिरशाह की तुलना सबसे कठोर है — एक आक्रांता भी प्रजा की बात सुन लेता था, पर 'सभ्य' अंग्रेज़ शासक नहीं। यह उस समय निडर पत्रकारिता का उदाहरण है।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: लोकतंत्र में जनता की आवाज़ सुनना शासक का कर्तव्य है। आज भी व्यंग्य (कार्टून, स्टैंड-अप, लेख) सत्ता से प्रश्न पूछने का माध्यम है — अभिव्यक्ति की स्वतंत्रता संविधान का अनुच्छेद 19(1)(a) देता है।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** शिवशंभु की दो गायों की कहानी के माध्यम से लेखक क्या कहना चाहते हैं?
**उत्तर:** शिवशंभु की दो गायें थीं — एक बलवती, एक कमज़ोर; बलवती गाय कमज़ोर को सींग मारती थी, फिर भी जब कमज़ोर गाय को दे दिया गया, तो बलवती उदास होकर बिछुड़ने के दुःख में चारा नहीं खाती थी। लेखक बताते हैं कि भारत में पशु भी विदाई पर दुखी होते हैं, फिर मनुष्यों का क्या कहना।

**प्रश्न:** कर्ज़न को इस्तीफ़ा क्यों देना पड़ गया?
**उत्तर:** कर्ज़न चाहते थे कि उनकी पसंद के एक सैनिक अफ़सर को एक पद पर नियुक्त किया जाए; इंग्लैंड की सरकार ने उनकी बात नहीं मानी, अपमानित होकर उन्होंने इस्तीफ़ा दिया।

steps.title: व्याकरण बिंदु
steps.body:
**व्यंग्य-युक्तियाँ**: आदरसूचक संबोधन ('माई लॉर्ड'), प्रश्नवाचक वाक्य, ऐतिहासिक तुलना।

**संधि**: शोक + आकुल = शोकाकुल; सम् + भाषण = संभाषण (अनुस्वार)।

steps.title: उत्तर लिखने की युक्ति
steps.body:
- पहले प्रश्न का मुख्य शब्द पहचानें।
- पाठ से एक घटना या पंक्ति का उदाहरण दें।
- छोटे प्रश्न में 3–4 वाक्य, बड़े प्रश्न में 6–7 वाक्य लिखें।

scenes.text: गाँव में धनराम लोहार की भट्ठी पर हथौड़े की ठक-ठक।
पुराना सहपाठी मोहन — पंडित का होनहार बेटा — हँसुवे की धार लगवाने आया।
फिर मोहन ने ख़ुद हथौड़ा उठाया और लोहे का गोल छल्ला गढ़ दिया!

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **शेखर जोशी** (1932–2022) 'नई कहानी' आंदोलन के कथाकार; जन्म अल्मोड़ा (उत्तराखंड)। श्रमिक और पहाड़ी जीवन पर कहानियाँ — 'कोसी का घटवार', 'दाज्यू'।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
**मोहन** पुरोहित **वंशीधर** का बेटा, गाँव के स्कूल का सबसे होनहार छात्र था। मास्टर **त्रिलोक सिंह** उसे मॉनीटर बनाते, और कमज़ोर छात्र **धनराम** (लोहार गंगाराम का बेटा) को मोहन से सज़ा दिलवाते। धनराम पढ़ाई छोड़ पिता का काम सीखने लगा।

मोहन को आगे पढ़ाने के लिए एक रिश्तेदार **रमेश** लखनऊ ले गया, पर वहाँ वह घर का नौकर बनकर रह गया, पढ़ाई पिछड़ गई; तकनीकी स्कूल का कोर्स भी काम न दिलाया, वह गाँव लौट आया। एक दिन हँसुवे की धार लगवाने वह **धनराम की दुकान** पहुँचा। धनराम एक मोटी छड़ को गोल करने की कोशिश कर रहा था, पर ठीक नहीं बन रहा था। मोहन ने हथौड़ा लेकर नपी-तुली चोटों से **सुडौल गोला** बना दिया। धनराम हैरान था — एक ब्राह्मण लोहार का काम कर रहा था; मोहन की आँखों में सृजन का आनंद था। **जाति का भेद लोहे की तरह गल गया**।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** धनराम मोहन को अपना प्रतिद्वंद्वी क्यों नहीं समझता था?
**उत्तर:** धनराम बचपन से मोहन को होनहार और श्रेष्ठ मानता था; जातिगत संस्कारों के कारण भी वह मोहन से बराबरी नहीं सोचता था। मोहन को मास्टर का विशेष स्नेह था, इसलिए वह उसे प्रतिद्वंद्वी नहीं, आदर्श मानता था।

**प्रश्न:** मोहन के लखनऊ आने के बाद के समय को लेखक ने उसके जीवन का एक नया अध्याय क्यों कहा है?
**उत्तर:** लखनऊ में उसका पढ़ाई का सपना टूट गया; वह रमेश के घर का नौकर बन गया, सामान्य स्कूल में पिछड़ गया, तकनीकी कोर्स भी काम न आया। उसका जीवन नई, कठिन दिशा में मुड़ गया।

**देशज/आंचलिक शब्द**: हँसुवा, आफ़र, धौंकनी।

**ध्वन्यात्मक शब्द**: ठक-ठक, खट-खट।

scenes.text: रात की आँधी में सचिवालय के लॉन का जामुन का पेड़ गिर गया।
सुबह माली ने देखा — पेड़ के नीचे एक आदमी दबा है, ज़िंदा!
फिर शुरू हुआ — फ़ाइल, विभाग, मीटिंग, विभाग, फ़ाइल…

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **कृश्न चंदर** (1914–1977) उर्दू-हिंदी के प्रसिद्ध कथाकार। प्रगतिशील लेखक; व्यंग्य और यथार्थ उनकी विशेषता। 'एक गधे की आत्मकथा', 'कालू भंगी' प्रसिद्ध। पद्म भूषण।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
सचिवालय के लॉन में जामुन का पेड़ गिरा, नीचे एक आदमी दबा था। क्लर्क और माली उसे निकालना चाहते थे, पर सुपरिंटेंडेंट ने कहा कि पहले संबंधित विभाग से अनुमति चाहिए। मामला **व्यापार विभाग** → **कृषि विभाग** → **हॉर्टीकल्चर विभाग** तक गया — कोई पेड़ काटने की अनुमति नहीं देता क्योंकि वह **फलदार** पेड़ था।

लोग कहते — आदमी को काटकर निकाल दो, **प्लास्टिक सर्जरी** विभाग उसे जोड़ देगा! जब पता चला कि दबा आदमी **कवि** है, तो फ़ाइल **कल्चरल डिपार्टमेंट** (साहित्य अकादमी) गई; उन्होंने उसे अकादमी का सदस्य बना दिया, पर पेड़ नहीं हटाया। फिर पता चला कि पेड़ **पीटोनिया** राज्य के प्रधानमंत्री ने लगाया था — अब **विदेश विभाग** का मामला; संबंध बिगड़ने का डर। अंत में प्रधानमंत्री ने ज़िम्मेदारी लेकर पेड़ काटने का आदेश दिया — पर जब फ़ाइल पूरी होकर पहुँची, तब तक **कवि की मृत्यु** हो चुकी थी। उसकी 'जीवन की फ़ाइल' भी पूरी हो गई।

steps.title: मुख्य बिंदु
steps.body:
- हास्य-व्यंग्य: लालफ़ीताशाही और संवेदनहीन नौकरशाही

- हर विभाग का ज़िम्मेदारी टालना
- कवि को अकादमी सदस्यता, पर जीवन-रक्षा नहीं
- करुण अंत — व्यवस्था की विफलता

steps.title: शब्द-अर्थ
steps.body:
- **सचिवालय** — सरकारी मुख्य कार्यालय (सेक्रेटेरिएट)
- **लालफ़ीताशाही** — अनावश्यक सरकारी नियम-प्रक्रिया से देरी
- **सुपरिंटेंडेंट** — अधीक्षक
- **हॉर्टीकल्चर** — बाग़बानी
- **अनुमति** — इजाज़त
- **संवेदनहीन** — भावनाशून्य
- **कल्चरल** — सांस्कृतिक

steps.title: वाक्य-प्रयोग
steps.body:

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- 'पीटोनिया' काल्पनिक राज्य है।

- साहित्य अकादमी ने कवि को **सदस्य** बनाया, बचाया नहीं।

steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: कृश्न चंदर एक असंभव-सी स्थिति (कई दिन तक पेड़ के नीचे दबा आदमी) बनाकर नौकरशाही की वास्तविकता दिखाते हैं — नियम मनुष्य की सेवा के लिए हैं, पर यहाँ मनुष्य नियमों की बलि चढ़ गया। हर विभाग 'हमारे अधिकार क्षेत्र में नहीं' कहकर पल्ला झाड़ता है। कवि को सदस्यता मिलना, पर जीवन नहीं — यह कला और कलाकार के प्रति दिखावटी सम्मान पर व्यंग्य है।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: आज भी आपदा, अस्पताल या प्रमाण-पत्र के मामलों में 'पहले फ़ॉर्म भरो' वाली सोच जान जोखिम में डालती है। आपातकाल में तुरंत 112 पर कॉल करें; 'गुड समैरिटन' नियम मदद करने वालों की रक्षा करते हैं।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** बेचारा जामुन का पेड़। कितना फलदार था। और इसकी जामुनें कितनी रसीली होती थीं। — यह संवाद कहानी के किस प्रसंग में आया है? इससे लोगों की कैसी मानसिकता का पता चलता है?
**उत्तर:** यह संवाद पेड़ गिरने के बाद क्लर्कों का है। उन्हें दबे हुए आदमी से ज़्यादा जामुन के पेड़ और उसके फलों की चिंता थी — इससे लोगों की संवेदनहीन, स्वार्थी मानसिकता का पता चलता है।

**प्रश्न:** दबा हुआ आदमी एक कवि है, यह बात कैसे पता चली और इस जानकारी का फ़ाइल की यात्रा पर क्या असर पड़ा?
**उत्तर:** माली से बातचीत में दबे आदमी ने ग़ालिब का शेर पढ़ा और बताया कि वह कवि है ('ओस के फूल' उसका संग्रह)। इसके बाद फ़ाइल कल्चरल डिपार्टमेंट गई, उसे साहित्य अकादमी का सदस्य बनाया गया, पर पेड़ नहीं हटा।

**सामासिक पद**: लालफ़ीताशाही; सचिवालय (सचिव + आलय, दीर्घ संधि)।

**मुहावरे**: 'पल्ला झाड़ना' = ज़िम्मेदारी से बचना; 'टाल-मटोल करना'।

school-c11-history.title: Class 11 History · Themes in World History
school-c11-history.description: Chapter-by-chapter companion to the Class 11 world-history syllabus: early cities, empires, nomads, medieval Europe, Renaissance, colonised peoples and East Asian modernisation — with timelines, maps described in words and source-based practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Writing and City Life
courses.summary: Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates: why cities first grew in the south, how writing began as bookkeeping, how temples, kings and trade shaped urban life, and what Mari, Uruk, Ur and Babylon tell us.
outcomes: Learners can locate Mesopotamia and describe its geography in words
Learners can explain the link between urbanisation and the invention of writing
Learners can describe temple economy, kingship and trade in Mesopotamian cities
Learners can answer source-based questions on Mari, Ur and the Gilgamesh epic

scenes.text: Around 3500 BCE a farmer in southern Iraq watches canal water spread across a flat, rainless plain.
His barley surplus travels to the temple at Uruk, where hundreds of people who never farm eat from it.

steps.title: The map in words
steps.body:
Mesopotamia (Greek: 'between rivers') is modern **Iraq**. The **Euphrates** (west) and **Tigris** (east) flow south-east from the Turkish highlands into the Persian Gulf.

- **North**: upland steppe with enough rain for farming and pasture (Assyria).
- **South**: flat alluvial plain, little rain, very fertile when irrigated — the region of the first cities (Sumer, Akkad).
- East: Zagros mountains of Iran; west: Syrian desert.

steps.title: Why cities began in the south
steps.body: Irrigation canals made the southern plain the most productive farmland in the region, creating **surplus**. But the south lacked stone, metal and good timber, so these had to be **traded** from Turkey, Iran and across the Gulf. Surplus + trade + organisation of labour = conditions for cities.

steps.title: Solved: 'Natural fertility is not enough'
steps.body:
**Q:** Why do historians say Mesopotamian prosperity also depended on organisation?

**A (steps):** 1) The rivers flooded unpredictably and sometimes shifted course. 2) Canals had to be dug and cleaned every year. 3) That needed coordinated labour and decisions on water sharing. 4) So temples and rulers that could organise labour became central — fertility plus management produced surplus.

steps.title: Solved: three types of urbanism
steps.body:
**Q:** Name three kinds of towns in Mesopotamia.

**A:** Towns that grew around **temples** (Uruk); towns that grew as **trade centres**; and **imperial/royal cities** (later Assyrian capitals such as Nineveh).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the rivers: Tigris is the **eastern** one.
- Saying cities grew because of rain — the south had very little rain; it was **irrigation**.
- Calling Mesopotamia 'Egypt' or placing it on the Nile.

activity.prompt: Match the place with its description

quiz.q: Mesopotamia today is mostly in which country?
quiz.why: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates lies mainly in modern Iraq.

quiz.q: The earliest cities of Mesopotamia arose in the:
quiz.why: Irrigation produced surplus on the southern alluvial plain.

quiz.q: Which resource did southern Mesopotamia lack and import?
quiz.why: Stone, metal and good wood came by trade.

quiz.q: Which river lies on the eastern side?
Why was organisation vital in Mesopotamia?
quiz.why: Canal-building and maintenance required organised labour.

scenes.text: A boy in a scribal school presses a reed stylus into wet clay to record '10 sheep'.
His teacher checks the signs — years of practice lie ahead before he can write letters and laws.

steps.title: From counting to cuneiform
steps.body:
The first tablets (Uruk, around **3200 BCE**) are lists of goods — grain, cattle, cloth — with numbers and pictorial signs. Writing began as **accounting** for the temple economy.

Around 2600 BCE the signs became wedge-shaped (**cuneiform**, Latin *cuneus* = wedge), written with a pointed reed on clay. The language was **Sumerian**, later **Akkadian**, which replaced Sumerian as the spoken language by about 2400 BCE.

steps.title: How the system worked
steps.body:
- A sign stood for a **syllable**, not a single letter, so there were hundreds of signs.
- Only a small trained group of scribes could write.
- Clay tablets survive well — tens of thousands have been found.
- Mesopotamians used a base-60 (**sexagesimal**) system — the origin of 60 minutes and 360 degrees.

steps.title: Solved: why did writing appear in cities?
steps.body: **A:** 1) Cities ran complex economies — goods flowed in and out of temples. 2) Memory could not track thousands of transactions. 3) Long-distance trade needed records of who sent what. 4) So writing answered an urban administrative need.

steps.title: Solved: uses of writing beyond accounts
steps.body: Writing was later used for **dictionaries, letters, legal contracts, royal inscriptions, astronomy, mathematics and literature** such as the Epic of Gilgamesh. Kings used it to proclaim their deeds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cuneiform is a **script**, not a language.
- It was written on **clay**, not papyrus (papyrus is Egypt).
- Literacy was **not** widespread.

statements.s: The earliest Mesopotamian tablets were mostly poems.
statements.why: They were lists of goods and numbers.

statements.s: Cuneiform signs were pressed into clay with a reed stylus.
Each cuneiform sign stood for a single alphabet letter.
Akkadian later replaced Sumerian as the spoken language.
Most ordinary people could read and write.

quiz.q: The earliest Mesopotamian writing (c. 3200 BCE) recorded:
The base-60 system survives today in:
Assertion: Literacy was limited in Mesopotamia. Reason: Hundreds of syllabic signs had to be learned.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
quiz.why: The complexity of the script restricted writing to trained scribes.

scenes.text: In Ur, houses huddle along narrow winding lanes; rubbish is thrown into the street and floors rise over time.
The royal tombs nearby hold gold, lyres and weapons — proof of a powerful elite.

steps.title: The temple at the centre
steps.body: Early temples began as small shrines and grew into large complexes with storerooms. The temple was the house of a god (e.g. moon god of Ur, Inanna of love and war). It **collected produce, organised weaving and oil-pressing, owned land and herds**, and was the first big employer.

steps.title: Rise of kings
steps.body: Frequent wars between city-states over land and water made successful **war leaders** powerful. They distributed loot, gave gifts to temples, took prisoners as labourers, and gradually became permanent **kings** who controlled temples and the economy. A famous early ruler, **Enmerkar** of Uruk, appears in legend sending for lapis lazuli from a distant land.

steps.title: Urban society
steps.body:
- Society had an elite (a small group owning much of the wealth — see Ur's royal tombs) and ordinary people.
- The **nuclear family** was the norm; fathers arranged marriages; inheritance passed to sons.
- Ur excavations (by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s–30s) show houses with an inner courtyard, rooms opening onto it, no windows to the street — privacy was valued.
- Town planning was **not** grid-like: streets were narrow and winding, no drainage system like Harappa.

steps.title: Solved source-style question
steps.body:
**Source idea:** Omens recorded at Ur: a raised threshold brings wealth; a front door that does not open towards another house brings luck.

**Q:** What do such beliefs tell us? **A:** 1) They show attention to privacy and fortune in house design. 2) Ordinary domestic life, not just kings, mattered to people. 3) Archaeology plus texts give a fuller picture.

steps.title: Solved: Mari — a city of herders and farmers
steps.body: Mari, on the **upper Euphrates** (c. 2000–1759 BCE), was a royal capital where farmers and pastoralists (Amorites, Akkadians, Aramaeans) met. Its huge palace of King **Zimrilim** had about 260 rooms. Mari taxed boats carrying goods — wood, copper, tin, oil, wine — moving between the south and Turkey/Syria. It was destroyed by Hammurabi of Babylon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Do not describe Ur with a grid plan or covered drains — that is Harappa.
- Mari is in the **north-west** (upper Euphrates), not the far south.

story.title: The last king who loved the past

scenes.text: Around 550 BCE, King Nabonidus of Babylon digs up an old statue at Ur and has it repaired.
Centuries earlier, Ashurbanipal of Assyria had collected tablets into a library at Nineveh.

steps.title: Babylon and Assyria
steps.body:
- **Hammurabi** (reigned c. 1792–1750 BCE) made Babylon the centre of the south and issued a famous law code.
- **Assyrian** kings ruled from the north (Nineveh) and built an empire; **Ashurbanipal** (7th century BCE) gathered a library of tablets on history, epics, omens and science at Nineveh.
- **Nabopolassar** freed Babylonia from Assyria (625 BCE); Babylon became a grand city of about 850 hectares with triple walls and a ziggurat. In **539 BCE** it fell to the Achaemenid Persians under Cyrus.

steps.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
steps.body: Gilgamesh, a ruler of Uruk, loses his friend Enkidu, searches for immortality, fails, and returns home consoled by the sight of the city walls his people built. The lesson: a person lives on through the **city and its people**. The epic shows how proud Mesopotamians were of their cities.

steps.title: Solved: legacy of Mesopotamia
steps.body: **Q:** State two lasting contributions. **A:** 1) **Calendar and time**: division of year into 12 months, hour into 60 minutes. 2) **Mathematics and astronomy**: multiplication and division tables, square roots, eclipses observed. 3) Most important: **writing and record-keeping** transmitted to later cultures.

steps.title: Solved: timeline reasoning
steps.body: Uruk tablets (c. 3200 BCE) → cuneiform (c. 2600 BCE) → Akkadian replaces Sumerian (c. 2400 BCE) → Hammurabi (c. 1792–1750 BCE) → Ashurbanipal's library (7th c. BCE) → Babylon falls to Persia (539 BCE). Notice BCE dates **count down** towards year 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In BCE, a **larger** number is **earlier**.
- Nineveh = Assyria (north); Babylon = south.
- Gilgamesh is a hero of **Uruk**, not Babylon.

quiz.why: The city and its people outlive the individual.

steps.title: How to answer a source question
steps.body: 1) Read the source twice. 2) Identify who wrote it, when, why. 3) Answer exactly what is asked (often 2 + 2 + 3 marks). 4) Link to the chapter concept (urbanisation, writing, kingship). 5) Do not just copy the source.

steps.title: Map answers
steps.body: Learn to mark: Tigris, Euphrates, Ur, Uruk, Babylon, Mari, Nineveh, Persian Gulf. Describe direction (north-west, south-east) in long answers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing everything you know instead of what the question asks; forgetting to name the city in a map-based answer.

courses.title: Ch 2 · An Empire Across Three Continents
courses.summary: The Roman Empire from Augustus to late antiquity: its geography across Europe, Asia and Africa, the Senate, army and emperor, the third-century crisis, economy and slavery, and the transformations under Diocletian and Constantine.
outcomes: Learners can describe the extent of the Roman Empire in words
Learners can explain the roles of emperor, Senate and army
Learners can analyse the third-century crisis and late-antique changes
Learners can use sources (coins, papyri, amphorae) to study the economy

scenes.text: A Roman soldier guards the Rhine frontier in 150 CE; letters from his family reach him from Egypt.
One empire stretches from Scotland to the Euphrates and from the Danube to the Sahara.

steps.title: The empire in words
steps.body: The Roman Empire surrounded the **Mediterranean** ('Our Sea'). North: the **Rhine and Danube** rivers formed the frontier. South: the **Sahara** desert. East: the **Euphrates**, beyond which lay the rival **Iranian empire** (Parthians, then **Sasanians** from 224 CE). It spanned **Europe, West Asia and North Africa** — three continents.

steps.title: Sources historians use
steps.body:
- **Texts**: histories, letters, speeches, laws.
- **Documents**: papyri from Egypt — contracts, accounts, letters.
- **Material remains**: buildings, coins, mosaics, pottery (amphorae).

steps.title: Solved: Roman vs Iranian empire
steps.body: **Q:** Compare the two empires. **A:** 1) Both were large, lasting empires and rivals fighting over the Euphrates frontier. 2) Rome was **culturally diverse** with Greek in the east and Latin in the west. 3) Iran under the Sasanians was centred on Mesopotamia and Iran. 4) The Mediterranean bound Rome together.

steps.title: Solved: languages
steps.body: The empire's two official/dominant languages were **Latin** (west) and **Greek** (east), but many local languages (Coptic, Aramaic, Punic, Celtic) survived.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not say Rome ruled India or China; its eastern edge was around the Euphrates. Parthians/Sasanians were rivals, not provinces.

activity.prompt: Match frontier to direction

quiz.q: The Mediterranean was called by Romans:

The empire spanned how many continents?

scenes.text: In 27 BCE Octavian becomes 'Augustus' but calls himself only 'first citizen' (princeps).
Behind the modest title stands a paid professional army.

steps.title: The Principate
steps.body: The regime founded by **Augustus** in **27 BCE** is called the **Principate**. The emperor was formally 'first citizen' to respect the **Senate**, which had held power in the Republic. In reality, power rested with the emperor.

steps.title: Three key players
steps.body:
- **Emperor**: ruled; succession often within family, natural or adoptive.
- **Senate**: wealthy aristocratic families; mostly hostile to emperors who were cruel or violent; wrote much of surviving history.
- **Army**: a **paid professional** force with 25 years' service — Rome's distinctive institution; could mutiny and decide emperors.

steps.title: Solved: why the army mattered
steps.body: **Q:** How did the army affect politics? **A:** 1) It was the largest organised body in the empire. 2) Soldiers wanted pay and good conditions, and agitated or mutinied. 3) In the third century, armies made and unmade emperors. So emperors had to keep it loyal.

steps.title: Solved: urbanisation and provinces
steps.body: Cities were the base of administration: the government collected taxes through city councils. By the early empire, provinces were tied together by cities such as Carthage, Alexandria and Antioch.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Principate ≠ Republic. The Senate did not disappear but lost real power.

activity.prompt: Who is it?

quiz.q: Most surviving Roman histories were written from the view of:
Assertion: The Roman army was a key political force. Reason: It was a paid professional army.
options: Both true; R doesn't explain A
quiz.why: Paid soldiers organised for their interests.

lessons.title: Economy, slaves and the third-century crisis

scenes.text: An amphora of Spanish olive oil reaches Rome; its broken shell joins Monte Testaccio, a hill made of millions of jars.
But in the 3rd century, wars on several fronts shake the empire.

steps.title: A sophisticated economy
steps.body: The empire had harbours, mines, quarries, brickyards, olive-oil factories. Wine, wheat and oil moved in **amphorae**. Spain's olive oil (in 'Dressel 20' jars) dominated, later rivalled by North Africa and Italy. Money economy: gold and silver coins; banking existed.

steps.title: Slavery and labour
steps.body: Slavery was deeply rooted, especially in Italy. As wars of conquest slowed (from the 1st century CE), slave supply fell, so owners turned to **slave breeding** or cheaper **seasonal free labour**. Writers advised treating workers carefully only for productivity. Free labour was also coerced in some places.

steps.title: The third-century crisis
steps.body: From the **230s**, the empire fought on many fronts: the **Sasanians** in the east (Shapur I claimed to have destroyed a 60,000-strong Roman army and captured Antioch), and **Germanic** groups (Alamanni, Franks, Goths) across the Rhine–Danube. In **47 years (235–284)** there were **25 emperors** — a sign of strain.

steps.title: Solved: amphorae as evidence
steps.body: **Q:** How do amphorae help historians? **A:** 1) Shapes identify origin (e.g. Spanish oil jars). 2) Distribution shows trade routes. 3) Changing proportions over time show which regions gained or lost markets.

steps.title: Solved: emperors count
steps.body: 25 emperors in 47 years → average reign under 2 years (47 ÷ 25 ≈ 1.9). This instability shows armies making and unmaking rulers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The third-century crisis is not the 'fall of Rome'; the empire recovered under Diocletian.

lessons.title: Late antiquity: Diocletian, Constantine and change

scenes.text: In 330 CE Constantine dedicates a new capital on the Bosphorus: Constantinople.
Merchants now count wealth in the gold solidus.

steps.title: Reforms
steps.body:
- **Diocletian** (284–305) reduced the empire's size where territories were not strategic, fortified frontiers, separated civil and military functions, and gave military commanders (duces) more autonomy.
- **Constantine** introduced the **solidus**, a gold coin of 4.5 g that remained in use for centuries, and founded **Constantinople** (modern Istanbul) in **330**.
- Christianity became the state religion in the 4th century.

steps.title: Late antiquity
steps.body: Historians use **late antiquity** for the 4th–7th centuries: the Roman world transformed — Christianity spread, a new aristocracy arose, the western empire fragmented into Germanic kingdoms (Visigoths, Franks, Lombards) in the 5th century, while the east (Byzantium) prospered. In the 7th century **Islam** rose and Arab armies took Egypt, Syria and much of Iran.

steps.title: Solved: why call it 'transformation' not 'fall'?
steps.body: 1) The eastern half continued to thrive with cities and trade. 2) Monetary stability returned with the solidus. 3) New religious and cultural forms emerged. 4) Only the political structure in the west collapsed.

steps.title: Solved: Constantine's coin
steps.body: The solidus had about 4.5 grams of pure gold and was minted in huge quantities — a sign of economic revival, not decline.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Constantinople ≠ Rome. Diocletian did not found Constantinople.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Nomadic Empires
courses.summary: The Mongols of the Central Asian steppe: social life, Genghis Khan's rise and campaigns, military organisation, the yasa, the yam courier system, and how his successors ruled from China to Russia.
outcomes: Learners can describe steppe pastoral society
Learners can narrate Genghis Khan's career with dates
Learners can explain the Mongol army's decimal organisation and the yam
Learners can evaluate the Mongol legacy using sources

scenes.text: A Mongol family packs its felt tent and herds sheep, horses and camels to summer pastures.
A harsh winter kills animals; raiding a settled town becomes tempting.

steps.title: The steppe in words
steps.body: Mongolia lies north of China's Great Wall: in the **west**, grassy steppe and the **Altai** mountains; in the **north**, forests; in the **south**, the **Gobi** desert. Rivers like the Onon and Selenga. Short summers, long harsh winters.

steps.title: Pastoralism and hunting
steps.body: Mongols were **pastoralists** (horses, sheep, goats, camels, cattle) and some were hunter-gatherers in the forest. Families lived in **kinship groups/clans** under chiefs. They traded with China for grain, metal tools, textiles; when trade was denied, they **raided**. China built walls to defend itself.

steps.title: Solved: why trade and raiding coexisted
steps.body: 1) The steppe could not produce grain or metal. 2) Agrarian China needed horses and furs. 3) Trade benefited both. 4) When China restricted trade or climate stress struck, nomads raided — so the relationship swung between commerce and conflict.

steps.title: Solved: why confederacies were fragile
steps.body: Pastoral alliances formed for war or crises but broke apart when the leader died or resources were scarce — so before Genghis Khan, large Mongol polities were short-lived.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Nomad' does not mean 'without society' — they had clans, chiefs, trade and law.

statements.s: The Gobi desert lies to the south of Mongolia.
Mongols grew most of their own grain.
China built walls partly to resist raids from the steppe.
Steppe confederacies before Genghis were usually long-lasting.

quiz.q: Case: a cold winter kills herds and China closes its markets. Likely result?

scenes.text: Born around 1162 near the Onon river, Temujin loses his father to poisoning and grows up in poverty.
In 1206 a great assembly (quriltai) proclaims him Genghis Khan, 'oceanic' or universal ruler.

steps.title: Rise to power
steps.body: Temujin (born **c. 1162**) built alliances — with his sworn brother **Jamuqa** (later an enemy) and with **Ong Khan** of the Kereits (later defeated). By **1206** he had united the Mongols and was proclaimed **Genghis Khan** at a quriltai.

steps.title: Campaigns
steps.body:
- **1209**: Tanggut (Xi Xia) in north-west China.
- **1215**: Beijing (Yanjing) sacked, Jin dynasty pushed south.
- **1218–1221**: **Khwarazm** empire in Central Asia after its ruler killed Mongol envoys — Otrar, Bukhara, Samarqand, Nishapur, Herat devastated.
- Pursuit of Sultan Jalaluddin to the **Indus**; Genghis did not cross into India.
- Died **1227**.

steps.title: Solved: why Khwarazm was attacked
steps.body: 1) Genghis sent envoys and traders. 2) Sultan Muhammad's governor at Otrar killed them. 3) Genghis retaliated (1219–1221) with a massive campaign. So the trigger was diplomatic insult; the motive included control of trade routes.

steps.title: Solved: date arithmetic
steps.body: Proclaimed 1206, died 1227 → ruled as Genghis Khan for **21 years**. Born c. 1162 → about 44 when proclaimed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Genghis Khan never conquered India; he turned back near the Indus. Don't confuse him with Kublai Khan (grandson, Yuan China).

activity.prompt: Order Genghis Khan's life

quiz.q: Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan in:
The killing of envoys at Otrar led to war against:
How many years did he rule as Genghis Khan?

scenes.text: A courier rides fresh horses from post to post, carrying an order thousands of km.
His paiza tablet entitles him to horses and food at every station.

steps.title: Decimal army
steps.body: Genghis Khan reorganised the army into units of **10, 100, 1,000** and **10,000 (tumen)**. Old tribal groupings were broken up and soldiers mixed — loyalty shifted from clan to Genghis Khan and his family. Mobile cavalry, mounted archery and winter campaigns on frozen rivers gave them speed.

steps.title: The yam
steps.body: The **yam** was a courier relay system with fresh horses and riders at posts. It was financed by a levy of animals from herders (the *qubcur* tax). It connected the empire for news, command and trade.

steps.title: The yasa
steps.body: **Yasa** originally meant law/decree; it became a code linked to Genghis Khan covering hunting, military organisation, postal system. Later successors used it to claim legitimacy and Mongol identity even as they adopted the religions and customs of the peoples they ruled.

steps.title: Solved: tumen arithmetic
steps.body: A tumen = 10 units of 1,000 = 100 units of 100 = 1,000 units of 10 = **10,000 soldiers**. Two tumens = 20,000.

steps.title: Solved: why mixing tribes mattered
steps.body: 1) Clan chiefs could no longer lead their own followers against him. 2) Soldiers' loyalty went to commanders appointed by Genghis. 3) This created a disciplined, unified army.

lessons.title: After Genghis: the successors and legacy

story.title: A merchant on the Silk Road

scenes.text: In the 1270s a caravan travels safely from the Black Sea to China under Mongol protection.
In Beijing, Kublai Khan rules as Yuan emperor of China.

steps.title: Expansion and limits
steps.body:
- **1236–1242**: Batu's campaigns in Russia, Poland and Hungary.
- **1258**: Hulegu sacks **Baghdad**, ending the Abbasid caliphate.
- **1260**: Mongols defeated by the **Mamluks** of Egypt at **Ain Jalut** — limit in the west.
- **Kublai Khan** completed conquest of China and founded the **Yuan** dynasty (Song fell 1279).

steps.title: Ulus division
steps.body: Genghis Khan divided his empire among sons as **ulus**: Jochi (west steppe, later Golden Horde), Chaghatai (Central Asia), Ogodei (became Great Khan), Toluy (Mongolia homeland; his sons Mongke, Kublai, Hulegu). Over time these became separate khanates.

steps.title: Administration and legacy
steps.body: Mongols relied on **sedentary administrators** — Chinese, Persian and Central Asian officials like the minister **Yelu Chucai** (Khitan). The **Pax Mongolica** made trade and travel across Eurasia safer. In Mongolia today Genghis Khan is a national hero.

steps.title: Solved: evaluate the legacy
steps.body: Devastation (destroyed cities, loss of life in Khwarazm) **and** integration (secure trade routes, exchange of technology and ideas, religious tolerance in many areas). A balanced answer weighs both.

steps.title: Solved: sources
steps.body: Sources include *The Secret History of the Mongols*, Persian chronicles (Juwaini, Rashid al-Din), Chinese records, and European travellers. Each had biases — Persian chroniclers under Mongol patronage often praised the rulers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ain Jalut (1260) was a Mongol **defeat**. Baghdad's sack was by Hulegu, not Genghis.

courses.title: Ch 4 · The Three Orders
courses.summary: Western European society from the 9th to 16th centuries: clergy, nobility and peasants; feudalism and the manor; monasteries; towns and cathedrals; and the 14th-century crisis of famine, Black Death and revolts.
outcomes: Learners can explain the 'three orders' and feudal relationships
Learners can describe the manor and peasant obligations
Learners can link technology, towns and cathedrals to economic change
Learners can analyse the 14th-century crisis and its consequences

lessons.title: Those who pray, fight and work

scenes.text: Around 1020, a French bishop writes that society has three orders: those who pray, those who fight, those who work.
Was this a description — or a justification?

steps.title: The three orders
steps.body:
- **First order: clergy** — priests, bishops, monks; Church owned vast land, collected the **tithe** (one-tenth of produce).
- **Second order: nobility** — knights and lords; held land (**fief**) from the king, gave military service.
- **Third order: peasants** — free peasants and **serfs** who worked the land.
The idea came from churchmen and justified inequality as God's plan.

steps.title: Feudalism
steps.body: From German *feud* = a piece of land. A **vassal** received a fief from a lord in return for loyalty and military service. Historian **Marc Bloch** (*Feudal Society*) emphasised studying the relationships and everyday life. Feudalism developed in France, England and Italy, especially after the Carolingian period.

steps.title: Solved: serf vs free peasant
steps.body: **Free peasant**: held land as a tenant, gave military service, paid taxes (e.g. *taille* in France). **Serf**: tied to the lord's land, could not leave, needed permission to marry, used the lord's mill/oven and paid fees. Both worked the lord's demesne some days per week.

steps.title: Solved: political timeline
steps.body: Charlemagne crowned emperor **800 CE**; Norman conquest of England **1066**; this brought French-style feudalism to England.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The 'three orders' was an ideal described by clergy, not an official census. Fief ≠ manor (a fief may contain manors).

activity.prompt: Which order?

items.text: Gave military service for a fief
Tied to the land as serfs

options: One-tenth of produce to the Church
Were tied to the lord's land

lessons.title: The manor, the knight and the monastery

scenes.text: Monks at Cluny pray at fixed hours; the abbey's lands stretch for miles.
Nearby a knight trains for war while serfs plough the lord's demesne.

steps.title: The manor
steps.body: A lord's manor had his house, demesne fields, pastures, forest, a church, mill and village. It was almost self-sufficient but needed salt, millstones and metal from outside. Peasants owed **labour services** on the demesne.

steps.title: Knights
steps.body: From the 9th century, local wars needed **cavalry**; knights held fiefs and fought for lords. Minstrels sang of their bravery — chivalry.

steps.title: Monasteries
steps.body: Monks took vows and lived apart. **St Benedict's** monastery in Italy (6th c.) had rules (73 chapters). **Cluny** (founded **910** in Burgundy) became a great centre. Later friars — **Franciscans and Dominicans** (13th c.) — moved among people preaching and living on charity.

steps.title: Solved: why the manor wasn't fully self-sufficient
steps.body: It lacked salt, millstones and metals, and lords wanted luxury goods — linking manors to trade and towns.

steps.title: Solved: monks vs friars
steps.body: Monks: enclosed in monasteries, fixed rules (Benedictine). Friars: wandered, preached, depended on alms (Franciscans, Dominicans).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Cluny is in France (Burgundy), not Italy; Benedict's original monastery was Monte Cassino in Italy.

items.back: Land kept by the lord and worked by peasants' labour services
Wandering preachers (Franciscans, Dominicans) living on charity
Code and ideal of knightly conduct praised by minstrels

quiz.q: Which was NOT produced on the manor?
Knights became important due to need for:

scenes.text: A peasant's horse, now with a horseshoe and shoulder-harness, pulls a heavy plough.
In town, masons spend decades building a Gothic cathedral with stained glass.

steps.title: Agricultural change (11th c.)
steps.body:
- Heavy iron-tipped **ploughs** and mouldboards.
- **Shoulder harness** and horseshoes let horses pull harder.
- **Three-field rotation**: one field winter crop (wheat/rye), one spring crop (peas, beans, oats), one fallow — land use rose from 1/2 to 2/3.
- Wind and water mills.
Result: more food, population growth, more trade.

steps.title: Towns and guilds
steps.body: Surplus revived towns. 'Town air makes free' — a serf who lived a year and a day in a town could become free. **Guilds** organised crafts, quality, prices. Fairs and merchants linked Europe.

steps.title: Cathedral towns
steps.body: From the 12th century, large **cathedrals** (e.g. Notre Dame, Paris — built over the 12th–13th centuries) were funded by Church, merchants and people. Stained glass told Bible stories to those who could not read.

steps.title: Solved: three-field arithmetic
steps.body: Two-field: half of land fallow → 1/2 cultivated. Three-field: one-third fallow → 2/3 cultivated. Increase = (2/3 − 1/2)/(1/2) = **33%** more land in use.

steps.title: Solved: why towns attracted serfs
steps.body: Freedom after a year and a day, paid work, guild membership — towns offered escape from labour services.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Three-field ≠ 'three crops on one field'. It rotates fields across seasons.

activity.prompt: A village has 300 acres. Under three-field rotation, how many acres are cultivated in a year?

quiz.q: Stained glass in cathedrals served to:

scenes.text: In 1347 ships arrive in Sicily carrying rats and fleas infected with plague.
In 1381 English peasants march on London demanding freedom.

steps.title: Crisis
steps.body:
- Colder climate after about 1300 shortened growing seasons; soil exhaustion; famines (1315–17).
- **Black Death** (1347–1350) killed an estimated 20% or more of Europe's population, much more in some towns.
- Labour shortage → peasants demanded higher wages; lords tried to restore old dues.

steps.title: Revolts
steps.body: Peasant revolts: Flanders (1323), **Jacquerie** in France (1358), **England 1381**. Though suppressed, they ended the old harsh labour services in many places.

steps.title: New monarchies
steps.body: 15th–16th centuries: kings strengthened power — **Louis XI** in France, **Maximilian** in Austria, **Henry VII** in England, **Isabelle and Ferdinand** in Spain. Standing armies, permanent bureaucracy, national taxation. Example: France's Estates-General (clergy, nobles, commoners) was called in 1614 and then not again until 1789.

steps.title: Solved: how did plague weaken feudalism?
steps.body: 1) Fewer workers → labour scarce. 2) Wages rose; peasants could bargain. 3) Lords' incomes fell. 4) Revolts showed resistance. 5) Money rents replaced labour services → serfdom declined in western Europe.

steps.title: Solved: interval
steps.body: Estates-General not called between 1614 and 1789 = **175 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Revolts did not 'win' outright; their long-term effect was weaker serfdom.

school-c11-maths-a.title: Class 11 Mathematics — Part A (Ch 1 to Ch 7)
school-c11-maths-a.description: All 14 chapters of Class 11 Mathematics, chapter by chapter, with solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes, chapter tests and a revision course with two mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Sets
courses.summary: Sets as well-defined collections: roster and set-builder forms, types of sets, subsets, power sets, intervals, Venn diagrams, operations and counting problems.
outcomes: Learners can write a set in roster and set-builder form
Learners can classify sets as empty, finite, infinite, equal or equivalent
Learners can find subsets, power sets and write intervals
Learners can perform union, intersection, difference and complement and use De Morgan's laws
Learners can solve counting problems with n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B)

lessons.title: What is a set? Representations and types

scenes.text: Coach Iqbal asks for 'the good players' in the class. Nobody agrees who is 'good'.
He changes it to 'students who scored 50+ runs this season'. Now everyone gets the same list — that is a set.

steps.title: Well-defined collections
steps.body:
A **set** is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. *Well-defined* means that for any object we can say clearly whether it belongs or not.

- 'Vowels of the English alphabet' is a set.
- 'Five most talented writers of India' is NOT a set (opinion-based).

Objects in a set are **elements**. We write a ∈ A ('a belongs to A') and b ∉ A.

steps.title: Roster form and set-builder form
steps.body:
- **Roster (tabular) form:** list elements in braces, separated by commas, without repetition: A = {a, e, i, o, u}. Order does not matter.
- **Set-builder form:** describe a common property: A = {x : x is a vowel of the English alphabet}.

The set of letters of 'SCHOOL' is {S, C, H, O, L} — the repeated O is written once.

steps.title: Types of sets
steps.body:
- **Empty (null, void) set** φ or { }: no elements, e.g. {x : x ∈ N, 1 < x < 2}.
- **Singleton:** exactly one element, e.g. {0}. Note {0} ≠ φ.
- **Finite set:** elements can be counted; n(A) is its cardinal number. **Infinite set:** not finite, e.g. N.
- **Equal sets:** exactly the same elements: {1,2,3} = {3,1,2}.
- **Equivalent sets:** same number of elements (n(A) = n(B)).

steps.title: Solved example 1: convert forms
steps.body:
Write {x : x is an integer and −3 ≤ x < 4} in roster form.

- Step 1: integers from −3 upward, stopping before 4.
- Step 2: {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3}.

Write {1, 4, 9, 16, 25} in set-builder form.
- Each element is a square: 1², 2², …, 5².
- Answer: {x : x = n², n ∈ N, 1 ≤ n ≤ 5}.

steps.title: Solved example 2: classify
steps.body:
Which are empty, finite or infinite?

- A = {x : x ∈ N and x² = 4} → x = 2 only → finite (singleton), n(A) = 1.
- B = {x : x is an even prime greater than 2} → no such number → empty set.
- C = {x : x is a point on a line} → infinitely many points → infinite.
- D = set of letters of 'FOLLOW' = {F, O, L, W} → finite, n(D) = 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing repeated elements: {L, O, L} should be {L, O}.
- Thinking {φ} is empty — it has ONE element (the empty set itself).
- Mixing ∈ (element) with ⊂ (subset): 2 ∈ {1,2} but {2} ⊂ {1,2}.
- Assuming order matters: {1,2} and {2,1} are equal.

steps.title: Standard symbols
steps.body: N natural numbers, Z integers, Q rationals, R reals, T irrationals, Z⁺ positive integers, Q⁺ positive rationals.

activity.prompt: Sort each collection.

quiz.q: Which of these is a set?
quiz.why: A set must be well-defined, so everyone agrees on what belongs. Odd natural numbers below 10 (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) is clear, but 'difficult', 'brave' and 'beautiful' are matters of opinion.

quiz.q: The roster form of {x : x ∈ N, x is a divisor of 6} is
quiz.why: The divisors of 6 that are natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and 6. Leaving out 6 or listing multiples (6, 12, 18…) is a mistake.
{φ} is a set holding one element, namely φ, so n({φ}) = 1. This differs from φ itself, which has 0 elements.
Both sets have 3 elements, so they are equivalent, but the elements differ (numbers versus letters), so they are not equal.

quiz.q: Number of distinct letters in 'ASSASSINATION' is
quiz.why: ASSASSINATION uses the letters A, S, I, N, T and O; repeats are not counted again in a set. That makes 6 distinct letters.

lessons.title: Subsets, power set, universal set and intervals

scenes.text: A pizza shop offers onion, corn and paneer. Riya wonders how many different pizzas are possible, including a plain one.
Each choice of toppings is a subset of {onion, corn, paneer}. There are 2³ = 8 of them.

steps.title: Subsets
steps.body:
A is a **subset** of B (A ⊂ B) if every element of A is also in B. If A ⊂ B and A ≠ B, A is a **proper subset**.

- φ is a subset of every set.
- Every set is a subset of itself.
- A = B exactly when A ⊂ B and B ⊂ A.
- N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R, and T ⊂ R; Q and T have nothing in common.

steps.title: Power set and universal set
steps.body:
The **power set** P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If n(A) = m, then n[P(A)] = 2^m.

A **universal set** U is the basic set containing all sets under discussion, e.g. for studying primes and even numbers, U could be N.

steps.title: Intervals as subsets of R
Solved example 1: power set
steps.body:
Find P(A) for A = {1, {2}}.

- Step 1: n(A) = 2 (the elements are 1 and the set {2}), so n[P(A)] = 4.
- Step 2: P(A) = {φ, {1}, {{2}}, {1, {2}}}.

steps.title: Solved example 2: intervals
steps.body:
Write {x : x ∈ R, −4 < x ≤ 6} as an interval and find its length.

- −4 is excluded (round bracket), 6 included (square bracket): (−4, 6].
- Length = 6 − (−4) = 10.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying {2} ∈ {1, 2}. Correct: {2} ⊂ {1, 2} and 2 ∈ {1, 2}.
- Forgetting φ and the set itself when listing subsets.
- Number of **proper** subsets is 2^m − 1, not 2^m.
- Writing ∞ with a square bracket.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: How many subsets does a set with 5 elements have? (32) How many proper subsets? (31)

activity.prompt: A set has 6 elements. How many elements does its power set have?

quiz.q: If A = {a, b, c}, the number of proper subsets of A is
quiz.why: A set with 3 elements has 2³ = 8 subsets. Proper subsets exclude the set itself, so 8 − 1 = 7.

options: φ ∈ A for every set A
φ ⊂ A for every set A
A ⊂ φ for every set A
quiz.why: The empty set φ is a subset of every set, so φ ⊂ A is true. φ ∈ A is not always true, and {φ} is not the same as φ.
A square bracket includes the endpoint and a round bracket excludes it, so [−3, 5) means −3 ≤ x < 5 with x real. The integer version would list only whole numbers.
A set with m elements has 2^m subsets, so 2^m = 16 gives m = 4. Hence n(A) = 4.

options: A = set of squares, B = set of rectangles
A = set of rectangles, B = set of squares
quiz.why: Every square is a rectangle, so the set of squares is a subset of the set of rectangles. The other pairs have the subset relation reversed or false.

lessons.title: Venn diagrams and operations on sets

scenes.text: In Class 11, some students are in the Art club, some in the Coding club, and a few in both.
Their teacher draws two overlapping circles inside a rectangle — a Venn diagram — to see every group at once.

steps.title: Union, intersection, difference
steps.body:
- **Union** A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — everything in at least one set.
- **Intersection** A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — common elements. If A ∩ B = φ, the sets are **disjoint**.
- **Difference** A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}. Note A − B ≠ B − A in general.

In a Venn diagram, U is a rectangle and sets are circles inside it.

steps.title: Complement and laws
steps.body:
**Complement** A′ = U − A = {x ∈ U : x ∉ A}.

Key laws:
- Commutative: A ∪ B = B ∪ A, A ∩ B = B ∩ A
- Associative and distributive: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C); A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
- Identity: A ∪ φ = A, A ∩ U = A; Idempotent: A ∪ A = A
- Complement: A ∪ A′ = U, A ∩ A′ = φ, (A′)′ = A, φ′ = U
- **De Morgan:** (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′

steps.title: Solved example 2: prove using elements
steps.body:
Show A − B = A ∩ B′.

- Let x ∈ A − B ⇔ x ∈ A and x ∉ B ⇔ x ∈ A and x ∈ B′ ⇔ x ∈ A ∩ B′.
- Since each step is reversible, the sets are equal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ — the operation flips: ∪ becomes ∩.
- Treating A − B and B − A as the same.
- Shading the whole circle for A − B instead of only the part outside B.
- Forgetting that the complement depends on U.

steps.title: Symmetric difference
steps.body: (A − B) ∪ (B − A) is the set of elements in exactly one of the two sets. It equals (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B).

activity.prompt: Match each set to its description.
pairs: In A but not in B
In U but not in A

quiz.why: A − B keeps the elements of A that are not in B. Removing 4 and 8 from {2, 4, 6, 8} leaves {2, 6}; 12 was never in A.
By De Morgan's law, the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. The union-complement (A ∪ B)′ is the one that equals A′ ∩ B′.
An element cannot be both in A and outside A, so A ∩ A′ has no elements and equals φ.
Two sets are disjoint when they share no element, that is A ∩ B = φ. A ∪ B = φ would need both sets to be empty.
Union distributes over intersection: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C). The option with intersection of A in front is the other distributive law for A ∩ (B ∪ C).

scenes.text: A survey of 100 students: 60 like tea, 45 like coffee, 20 like both.
The principal asks: how many like neither? A Venn diagram and one formula answer it in seconds.

steps.title: The key formulas
steps.body:
For finite sets:
- n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
- If A, B disjoint: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B)
- n(A − B) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B)
- n(A′) = n(U) − n(A)
- Three sets: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(A∩C) + n(A∩B∩C)

steps.title: Solved example 2: three languages
steps.body:
In a group of 50: 25 speak Hindi (H), 20 English (E), 15 Tamil (T); 8 speak H and E, 6 speak E and T, 5 speak H and T, 3 speak all three. How many speak none?

- Step 1: n(H ∪ E ∪ T) = 25 + 20 + 15 − 8 − 6 − 5 + 3 = 44.
- Step 2: none = 50 − 44 = **6**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding n(A) + n(B) without subtracting the overlap (double counting).
- In three-set problems, forgetting to add back n(A∩B∩C).
- Confusing 'only A' (A − B) with 'A'.
- Not checking that the region counts add up to n(U).

steps.title: Where this is used
steps.body: Survey analysis, database queries (SQL UNION and INTERSECT), probability of 'A or B' — the same inclusion–exclusion idea returns in Chapter 14.

activity.prompt: In a class of 40, 25 play cricket, 18 play football and 8 play both. How many play neither?

quiz.q: If n(A) = 20, n(B) = 15, n(A ∪ B) = 30, then n(A ∩ B) is
If n(U) = 50 and n(A) = 18, then n(A′) is
quiz.why: The complement contains everything in U not in A, so n(A′) = n(U) − n(A) = 50 − 18 = 32.

quiz.q: If n(A) = 12, n(A ∩ B) = 5, then n(A − B) is
quiz.why: n(A − B) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B) = 12 − 5 = 7, the elements in A but not in B.

quiz.q: For disjoint A and B with n(A) = 9, n(B) = 4, n(A ∪ B) =
quiz.why: Disjoint sets have no common element, so n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) = 9 + 4 = 13. There is nothing to subtract.

quiz.q: In the three-set formula, n(A ∩ B ∩ C) is
quiz.why: In n(A ∪ B ∪ C), the triple overlap is added three times and subtracted three times (in the pair overlaps), so it is missing and must be added back once at the end.

questions.q: Which of the following is a well-defined collection?
questions.why: A collection is well-defined if membership is objective. Even integers between 1 and 15 (2, 4, …, 14) is clear, while 'hard', 'good' and 'tall' depend on opinion.
Factor x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 2 or 3. Hence A = {2, 3}.

questions.q: The number of subsets of {a, b, c, d} is
questions.why: A set with 4 elements has 2⁴ = 16 subsets. 15 would be the number of proper non-empty subsets, not all subsets.
The complement of the complement of A gives back A, because taking 'not' twice undoes itself.
In (2, 7] the round bracket excludes 2 and the square bracket includes 7. So the interval contains 7 but not 2.

questions.q: If A ⊂ B, then A ∩ B is
questions.why: If A ⊂ B, every element of A is also in B, so the common part A ∩ B is just A.

questions.q: If A ⊂ B, then A ∪ B is
questions.why: If A ⊂ B, then everything in A is already in B, so A ∪ B adds nothing new and equals B.

options: Both true but R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true: a belongs to {a, b}. {a} is a subset exactly because its only element a is in {a, b}, so R explains A.
A ∩ B is the part of A shared with B. Taking it away from A leaves only the elements of A not in B, which is A − B.

questions.q: If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 5 with A ⊂ B, n(A ∪ B) is
questions.why: Since A ⊂ B, all elements of A are already in B, so A ∪ B = B and n(A ∪ B) = 5. Adding 3 + 5 would double count.
Elements in the union but not in the intersection are those in exactly one set, i.e. (A − B) ∪ (B − A). This is the symmetric difference.

questions.q: Case: In a town of 10,000 families, 40% read paper A, 20% read B, 10% read C, 5% read A and B, 3% B and C, 4% A and C, 2% all three. How many families read none?
questions.why: By inclusion–exclusion: 40 + 20 + 10 − 5 − 3 − 4 + 2 = 60% read at least one paper. So 40% read none, and 40% of 10,000 = 4000.

questions.q: In a group of 70 people, 37 like coffee, 52 like tea, and each person likes at least one. How many like both?
questions.why: Everyone likes at least one drink, so n(C ∪ T) = 70. Then n(C ∩ T) = 37 + 52 − 70 = 19.

questions.q: If n(A) = 4, the number of elements of P(P(A)) is
questions.why: n(P(A)) = 2⁴ = 16, and the power set of that has 2¹⁶ elements. 2⁸ or 2⁴ would stop one step early or compute wrongly.

questions.q: For sets A, B: A ∩ (A ∪ B) equals
questions.why: A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A by the absorption law: every element of A is in A ∪ B, so the common part is A itself.

questions.q: In a survey of 60 people, 25 read newspaper H, 26 read T, 26 read I, 9 read H and I, 11 read H and T, 8 read T and I, 3 read all. How many read exactly one newspaper?

courses.title: Ch 2 · Relations and Functions
courses.summary: Ordered pairs and Cartesian products, relations with domain, codomain and range, functions and their standard graphs, and the algebra of real functions.
outcomes: Learners can form Cartesian products and count their elements
Learners can represent relations and find domain and range
Learners can decide whether a relation is a function
Learners can sketch identity, constant, polynomial, modulus, signum and greatest-integer functions
Learners can add, subtract, multiply and divide real functions

scenes.text: Arjun has 3 shirts {red, blue, white} and 2 trousers {black, grey}.
Each outfit is an ordered pair (shirt, trouser). The list of all 6 outfits is a Cartesian product.

steps.title: Ordered pairs and A × B
steps.body:
An **ordered pair** (a, b) has a first and second element; (a, b) = (c, d) only when a = c and b = d.

The **Cartesian product** A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}.
- If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq.
- If A or B is empty, A × B = φ.
- A × B ≠ B × A in general.
- R × R = R² is the coordinate plane; R × R × R is space.

steps.title: Solved example 1: equal ordered pairs
steps.body:
Find x and y if (x + 1, y − 2) = (3, 1).

- First components equal: x + 1 = 3 → x = 2.
- Second components equal: y − 2 = 1 → y = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating (2, 3) as equal to (3, 2).
- Writing n(A × B) = p + q instead of pq.
- Forgetting that A × (B ∩ C) = (A × B) ∩ (A × C) is a property of products, not of pairs.

steps.title: Triplets
steps.body: A × A × A = {(a, b, c) : a, b, c ∈ A}. If n(A) = 2, it has 2³ = 8 ordered triplets.

activity.prompt: If n(A) = 4 and n(B) = 3, how many elements does A × B have?

quiz.why: Ordered pairs are equal when matching components are equal. So a = 3 and 1 = b, giving a = 3, b = 1.

quiz.q: If A = {x, y}, then A × A has how many elements?
quiz.why: The Cartesian product has n(A) × n(B) elements: 2 × 2 = 4, namely (x,x), (x,y), (y,x), (y,y).

quiz.q: If A × B = {(p, q), (p, r), (m, q), (m, r)}, then B is
quiz.why: In A × B the first components form A and the second components form B. The second components here are q and r, so B = {q, r}.

quiz.q: If A = φ, then A × B is
quiz.why: With A empty there is no first element to pair, so A × B has no pairs and equals φ.

quiz.q: Number of elements in A × A × A when n(A) = 3 is
quiz.why: A × A × A has n(A)³ elements, so 3³ = 27 ordered triples.

scenes.text: Out of all pairs of students, the class lists only those pairs who are siblings.
Picking some pairs out of a Cartesian product, by a rule, is exactly what a relation does.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **relation** R from A to B is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R we write a R b; b is the **image** of a and a the **pre-image** of b.

- **Domain:** set of first elements of R.
- **Codomain:** the whole set B.
- **Range:** set of second elements actually used; range ⊆ codomain.
- Representations: set-builder, roster, arrow diagram.

steps.title: Counting relations
steps.body: If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then A × B has pq elements, so the number of relations from A to B = number of subsets = **2^(pq)** (including the empty relation).

steps.title: Solved example 2: counting
steps.body:
A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 4}. Number of relations from A to B?

- n(A × B) = 4.
- Relations = 2⁴ = **16**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the codomain the range: the range contains only images that occur.
- Including pairs whose components are outside the given sets.
- Using 2^(p+q) instead of 2^(pq).

activity.prompt: Complete the counting rule.
activity.text: If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 2, the number of relations from A to B is 2 to the power ___ = ___.

quiz.q: R = {(x, x²) : x is a prime less than 10}. Range of R is
quiz.why: The primes below 10 are 2, 3, 5, 7. Squaring each gives 4, 9, 25, 49, which is the range (the set of second components).

quiz.q: A relation from A to B is a subset of
quiz.why: By definition, a relation from A to B is any subset of the Cartesian product A × B.

quiz.q: If n(A) = 2, n(B) = 3, the number of relations from A to B is
quiz.why: A × B has 2 × 3 = 6 pairs, and a relation is any subset of them, so there are 2⁶ = 64 relations.
The domain is the set of first components of the pairs, which are 1, 2 and 3. The second components 2, 4, 6 form the range.

quiz.q: The range of a relation is always
quiz.why: The range holds only the values actually reached, so it is a subset of the codomain. It need not equal the codomain.

scenes.text: Press a button on a vending machine and you get exactly one drink — never two, never a random one.
A rule that gives every input exactly one output is a function.

steps.title: What makes a relation a function
steps.body:
A relation f from A to B is a **function** if every element of A has **exactly one** image in B. Write f : A → B, y = f(x).

- Domain = A, codomain = B, range = {f(x) : x ∈ A}.
- A **real function** has domain and range that are subsets of R.
- Graph test: a vertical line meets the graph of a function at most once.

steps.title: Standard real functions
steps.body:
- **Identity** f(x) = x, range R (line y = x).
- **Constant** f(x) = c, range {c} (horizontal line).
- **Polynomial** f(x) = a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙxⁿ, e.g. x² (parabola), x³.
- **Rational** f(x)/g(x), g(x) ≠ 0, e.g. 1/x (domain R − {0}).
- **Modulus** |x| = x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0 (V-shape, range [0, ∞)).
- **Signum** sgn x = 1 (x > 0), 0 (x = 0), −1 (x < 0); range {−1, 0, 1}.
- **Greatest integer** [x] = greatest integer ≤ x, e.g. [2.7] = 2, [−1.3] = −2; step graph, range Z.

steps.title: Solved example 1: is it a function?
steps.body:
Which relations from A = {1,2,3} are functions?

- R₁ = {(1,4), (2,5), (3,6)} → each input has one image → **function**.
- R₂ = {(1,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7)} → 1 has two images → **not** a function.
- R₃ = {(1,4), (2,4)} → 3 has no image → **not** a function from A.

steps.title: Solved example 2: domain and range
steps.body:
f(x) = √(9 − x²).

- Need 9 − x² ≥ 0 → −3 ≤ x ≤ 3. Domain = [−3, 3].
- 9 − x² ranges from 0 to 9, so √ ranges from 0 to 3. Range = [0, 3].

g(x) = 1/(x − 2): domain R − {2}; range R − {0}.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- [−2.5] is −3, not −2 (move left on the number line).
- Two inputs with the same output is allowed; one input with two outputs is not.
- Forgetting to exclude zeros of the denominator from the domain.
- Confusing range with codomain.

steps.title: Use the graph plotter
steps.body: Plot |x|, [x] and sgn x in the Graph plotter lab and compare their shapes.

activity.prompt: Match the function with its range.

quiz.why: [x] is the greatest integer less than or equal to x. For −3.2 the integers below it are −4, −5, …, and the greatest is −4, not −3.
The function is undefined where the denominator x² − 4 = 0, that is x = ±2. So the domain is all real numbers except −2 and 2.

quiz.q: Which relation is a function on {1, 2}?
quiz.why: A function gives each element of the domain exactly one image. {(1, 3), (2, 3)} gives 1 and 2 one image each; the others miss an element or give 1 or 2 two images.
|x − 1| is never negative and equals 0 at x = 1, and grows without bound. So the range is [0, ∞).
The signum function gives −1 for negative inputs, 0 at 0 and 1 for positive inputs. Since −7 < 0, sgn(−7) = −1.

scenes.text: A shop's revenue is R(x) = 50x and its cost is C(x) = 20x + 300 for x items.
Profit P(x) = R(x) − C(x) = 30x − 300: subtracting functions is everyday business.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
For f, g : X → R:
- (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
- (f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x)
- (fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x)
- (αf)(x) = α f(x) for a real α
- (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x), only where g(x) ≠ 0

The domain of the result is the common domain (minus zeros of g for a quotient).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
f(x) = √x, g(x) = x (x ≥ 0).

- (f + g)(x) = √x + x, domain [0, ∞).
- (f/g)(x) = √x / x = 1/√x, domain (0, ∞) because g(0) = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (fg)(x) as f(g(x)) — product is not composition.
- Forgetting to remove points where g(x) = 0 in f/g.
- Simplifying f/g and then using the simplified domain.

activity.prompt: If f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1, find (fg)(2).

quiz.q: If f(x) = 3x and g(x) = x², (f − g)(2) =
Domain of (f/g) where f(x) = x, g(x) = x − 5 is
quiz.why: For f/g, we need g(x) ≠ 0. Since g(x) = x − 5 is zero at x = 5, the domain is R − {5}.
(2f)(x) = 2·f(x) = 2(x² + 1) = 2x² + 2. The multiplier applies to the whole function, including the constant.
(fg)(x) is the pointwise product f(x)·g(x). Composition, such as f(g(x)), is written f∘g, not fg.

quiz.q: If f(x) = x³ and g(x) = x, (f/g)(x) for x ≠ 0 is
quiz.why: (f/g)(x) = x³ ÷ x = x² for x ≠ 0, by cancelling one factor of x.

questions.why: Equal ordered pairs need equal components: x − 1 = 4 gives x = 5 and y + 2 = 7 gives y = 5. So x + y = 10.

questions.q: If n(A) = 3, n(B) = 4, then n(A × B) =
questions.why: n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B) = 3 × 4 = 12. Adding them would give 7, which is wrong for a Cartesian product.
[x] is the greatest integer not exceeding x. For 4.99 that is 4, since 5 is larger than 4.99.

questions.q: Which is not a function from {1, 2, 3}?
questions.why: A function must assign an image to every element of the domain. {(1, a), (2, b)} leaves 3 without an image, so it is not a function from {1, 2, 3}.
Since |x| ≥ 0, we get 2 − |x| ≤ 2, and the value 2 occurs at x = 0 with arbitrarily small values for large |x|. So the range is (−∞, 2].
The square root needs a non-negative input, so x − 3 ≥ 0, giving x ≥ 3. The domain is [3, ∞), with 3 included.

questions.q: Number of relations from a 3-element set to a 3-element set is
questions.why: A × B has 3 × 3 = 9 pairs, and each relation is a subset of those pairs, giving 2⁹ relations.

questions.q: Assertion: R = {(1, 2), (1, 3)} is not a function from {1} to {2, 3}. Reason: an element of the domain has two images.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the element 1 is paired with both 2 and 3, so one domain element has two images, and that is exactly why the relation is not a function.
f(−1) = (−1)² − 3(−1) + 1 = 1 + 3 + 1 = 5. The sign mistake −3(−1) = −3 gives a wrong answer.
The second components of A × B are 1, 2 and 3, so B = {1, 2, 3} and n(B) = 3. (A = {a, b} has 2 elements; 2 × 3 = 6 pairs.)

questions.q: Range of f(x) = x²/(1 + x²) is
questions.why: f(0) = 0 and x²/(1 + x²) is always less than 1 but gets closer to it as x grows. So the range is [0, 1), including 0 but never reaching 1.
The function is undefined where the denominator is zero. x² − 8x + 12 = (x − 2)(x − 6) = 0 at x = 2 and 6, so the domain is R − {2, 6}.

questions.q: Case: A taxi charges ₹50 fixed plus ₹12 per km. Fare f(d) for d km. What is f(15) and is f linear?
questions.why: Fare = fixed charge + rate × distance, so f(d) = 50 + 12d, which is linear in d. Then f(15) = 50 + 12 × 15 = 50 + 180 = ₹230.

questions.q: If f(x) = x + 1/x, then f(x)² − f(x²) equals
questions.why: f(x)² = (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x², and f(x²) = x² + 1/x². Subtracting gives 2.
Let [x] = n (an integer). Then x = (n + 1)/2, and n ≤ x < n + 1 gives −1 < n ≤ 1, so n = 0 (x = 1/2) or n = 1 (x = 1). Both check.

questions.q: For f(x) = |x| + |x − 2|, the minimum value is
questions.why: For 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, |x| + |x − 2| = x + (2 − x) = 2, and for x outside this interval the sum is bigger. So the minimum value is 2.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Trigonometric Functions
courses.summary: Degree and radian measure, trigonometric functions of any real number through the unit circle, signs and periodicity, compound-angle identities, multiple-angle and sum-to-product formulas.
outcomes: Learners can convert between degrees and radians and use l = rθ
Learners can evaluate trigonometric functions of any angle using signs and periodicity
Learners can apply sum and difference formulas
Learners can use double, triple-angle and transformation formulas to prove identities

scenes.text: A clock pendulum 75 cm long swings through an arc of 21 cm.
Tara wants the angle of swing. Arc ÷ radius gives it directly in radians: 21/75 = 0.28 rad.

steps.title: Measuring angles
steps.body:
An angle is the amount of rotation of a ray about its initial point; anticlockwise is positive.

- **Degree:** 1/360 of a full turn; 1° = 60′ (minutes), 1′ = 60″ (seconds).
- **Radian:** the angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal in length to the radius.
- For an arc of length l in a circle of radius r: **l = rθ** (θ in radians).
- A full turn = 2π rad = 360°, so **π rad = 180°**.

steps.title: Conversion
steps.body:
- Radian measure = (π/180) × degree measure
- Degree measure = (180/π) × radian measure
- 1 rad ≈ 57°16′ (using π ≈ 22/7), 1° ≈ 0.01746 rad.
- Useful: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 270° = 3π/2.

steps.title: Solved example 2: arc length
steps.body:
In a circle of radius 20 cm, find the arc subtending 45° at the centre (π = 22/7).

- Step 1: θ = 45° = π/4 rad.
- Step 2: l = rθ = 20 × π/4 = 5π = 5 × 22/7 ≈ **15.71 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using l = rθ with θ in degrees — it works only in radians.
- Writing 'π = 180' without units: π *radians* = 180°.
- Forgetting to change minutes into fractions of a degree before converting.

steps.title: Clock hands
steps.body: The minute hand moves 360° in 60 min = 6° per minute; the hour hand moves 0.5° per minute.

activity.prompt: Convert 6 radians to degrees, correct to the nearest degree (use π = 22/7).

quiz.why: 47°30′ = 47.5°. Multiply by π/180: 47.5π/180 = 95π/360 = 19π/72, and the negative sign stays, giving −19π/72.

quiz.q: The arc length for θ = 1.5 rad and r = 4 cm is
quiz.why: Arc length l = rθ when θ is in radians: 4 × 1.5 = 6 cm.

quiz.q: Angle turned by the minute hand in 20 minutes is
quiz.why: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, i.e. 6° per minute, so 20 minutes give 120°. In radians that is 120 × π/180 = 2π/3.
1 radian = 180°/π ≈ 57.27°, which is about 57°16′. It is not 60° or 45°.

scenes.text: A seat on a Ferris wheel goes round and round. Its height keeps repeating every turn.
That repeating height is a sine curve — trigonometric functions are made for things that go round.

steps.title: Unit-circle definition
steps.body:
Take the unit circle x² + y² = 1. If the arc from (1, 0) to point P(a, b) has length x (radians), define **cos x = a** and **sin x = b**.

- sin²x + cos²x = 1 for every x.
- tan x = sin x / cos x (x ≠ (2n + 1)π/2), cot x = cos x / sin x (x ≠ nπ), sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x.
- 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x.

steps.title: Signs, domain, range, period
steps.body:
Signs by quadrant: **I** all positive · **II** sin, cosec positive · **III** tan, cot positive · **IV** cos, sec positive.

- sin x and cos x: domain R, range [−1, 1], period 2π.
- tan x: domain R − {(2n+1)π/2}, range R, period π.
- sin(−x) = −sin x, cos(−x) = cos x (cos is even).
- sin x = 0 ⇔ x = nπ; cos x = 0 ⇔ x = (2n + 1)π/2.

steps.title: Solved example 1: finding the other five
steps.body:
cos x = −3/5 and x lies in Quadrant III. Find the others.

- sin²x = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25; in QIII sin is negative: sin x = −4/5.
- tan x = (−4/5)/(−3/5) = 4/3; cot x = 3/4.
- sec x = −5/3; cosec x = −5/4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the sign from the quadrant after using sin²x + cos²x = 1.
- Assuming tan has period 2π only — its fundamental period is π.
- Writing sin(−x) = sin x.
- Thinking sec x can be 1/2: |sec x| ≥ 1 always.

activity.prompt: In which quadrant is the angle if…

quiz.why: Subtract full turns: 765° = 2 × 360° + 45°, so sin 765° = sin 45° = 1/√2.

quiz.q: If sin x = 3/5 and x is in QII, tan x =
quiz.why: sin x = 3/5 gives |cos x| = 4/5. In the second quadrant cos is negative, so cos x = −4/5 and tan x = (3/5)/(−4/5) = −3/4.

quiz.q: The range of sin x is
quiz.why: On the unit circle, sin x is the y-coordinate, which ranges from −1 to 1 and reaches both ends. So the range is [−1, 1].
−1410° = −4 × 360° + 30°, so it is coterminal with 30°. Then cosec(−1410°) = cosec 30° = 1/sin 30° = 2.

quiz.q: The fundamental period of tan x is
quiz.why: The tangent repeats every π, since tan(x + π) = tan x. So its fundamental period is π, not 2π.

scenes.text: Kabir needs sin 15° exactly, but it is not in the table.
Since 15° = 45° − 30°, a difference formula builds it from two values he knows.

steps.title: The core identities
steps.body:
- cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y
- cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y
- sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y
- sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y
- tan(x ± y) = (tan x ± tan y)/(1 ∓ tan x tan y)
- cot(x ± y) = (cot x cot y ∓ 1)/(cot y ± cot x)

steps.title: Allied angles (from the formulas)
steps.body:
- cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x
- cos(π/2 + x) = −sin x, sin(π/2 + x) = cos x
- cos(π − x) = −cos x, sin(π − x) = sin x
- cos(π + x) = −cos x, sin(π + x) = −sin x
- cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- sin(x + y) ≠ sin x + sin y.
- In cos(x + y) the sign is MINUS; in cos(x − y) it is PLUS.
- Losing the sign in allied angles: work out the quadrant first, then the function (sin ↔ cos only for π/2 and 3π/2).

steps.title: Proof idea
steps.body: cos(x + y) is proved on the unit circle by equating two chord lengths (P₁P₃ and P₂P₄); all other formulas follow by substitution.

activity.prompt: Match each expression to its value.

quiz.why: cos(π/2 + x) = cos(π/2)cos x − sin(π/2)sin x = 0 − sin x = −sin x.
The expression matches sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B with A = 75° and B = 15°, giving sin 90° = 1.
tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B). With tan π/4 = 1, this gives (1 + tan x)/(1 − tan x).
cos 105° = cos(60° + 45°) = cos60 cos45 − sin60 sin45 = (1/2)(1/√2) − (√3/2)(1/√2) = (√2 − √6)/4. It is negative, since 105° is in the second quadrant.
sin(π − x) = sin x, because the angle lies in the second quadrant, where sine is positive.

scenes.text: Two tuning forks with slightly different notes sound together, and you hear a 'wah-wah' beat.
The sum sin a + sin b turning into a product of sine and cosine explains the beat — a transformation formula.

steps.title: Double and triple angles
steps.body:
- sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 tan x/(1 + tan²x)
- cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x)
- tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x)
- sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x
- cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x
- tan 3x = (3 tan x − tan³x)/(1 − 3 tan²x)

steps.title: Sum ↔ product
steps.body:
- cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x+y)/2) cos((x−y)/2)
- cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x+y)/2) sin((x−y)/2)
- sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x+y)/2) cos((x−y)/2)
- sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x+y)/2) sin((x−y)/2)

Reverse forms: 2 cos x cos y = cos(x+y) + cos(x−y); −2 sin x sin y = cos(x+y) − cos(x−y); 2 sin x cos y = sin(x+y) + sin(x−y).

steps.title: Solved example 1: double angle values
steps.body:
tan x = 3/4 and x is in QIII. Find sin 2x, cos 2x, tan 2x.

- In QIII: sin x = −3/5, cos x = −4/5.
- sin 2x = 2(−3/5)(−4/5) = **24/25**.

Prove (sin 5x + sin 3x)/(cos 5x + cos 3x) = tan 4x.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
courses.summary: Why we need i = √−1, the algebra of complex numbers, conjugate and modulus, the Argand plane and polar form, and solving quadratic equations with negative discriminant.
outcomes: Learners can write complex numbers as a + ib and use powers of i
