lessons.title: The number i and the algebra of complex numbers

scenes.text: Neha tries x² + 1 = 0. No real number squared gives −1.
Mathematicians invented i with i² = −1 — and an entire number system, used today in electrical engineering, opened up.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Let **i = √−1**, so i² = −1. A **complex number** is z = a + ib with a, b real: Re z = a, Im z = b.

- Purely real: b = 0; purely imaginary: a = 0.
- a + ib = c + id ⇔ a = c and b = d.
- Powers of i repeat every 4: i, −1, −i, 1. So i^n depends on n mod 4. For example i^4k = 1.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
For z₁ = a + ib, z₂ = c + id:
- Sum: (a + c) + i(b + d); difference: (a − c) + i(b − d)
- Product: (ac − bd) + i(ad + bc)
- Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative; 0 is the additive identity and 1 the multiplicative identity.
- Identities like (z₁ + z₂)² = z₁² + 2z₁z₂ + z₂² still hold.

steps.title: Solved example 1: powers of i
steps.body:
Find i⁻³⁵.

- i⁻³⁵ = 1/i³⁵ = 1/(i³²·i³) = 1/i³ = 1/(−i).
- Multiply by i/i: i/(−i²) = i/1 = **i**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- √(−4)·√(−9) is NOT √36 = 6. Correct: (2i)(3i) = 6i² = −6. The rule √a√b = √(ab) fails when both are negative.
- Treating i as a variable and forgetting i² = −1.
- Saying one complex number is 'greater' than another — order is not defined for complex numbers.

activity.prompt: Find the real part of (1 + 2i)(3 − i).

quiz.why: Powers of i repeat every 4. 103 = 4 × 25 + 3, so i¹⁰³ = i³ = −i.
Add real parts and imaginary parts separately: (2 + 4) + (3 − 5)i = 6 − 2i.
Two complex numbers are equal when their real and imaginary parts match. So x = 3 and y = −7, giving (3, −7).

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations)

lessons.title: Conjugate, modulus and division

scenes.text: Dividing by 3 + 4i looks scary until Sam multiplies top and bottom by 3 − 4i.
The denominator becomes 25, a real number. The trick is the conjugate.

steps.title: Conjugate and modulus
steps.body:
For z = a + ib:
- **Conjugate** z̄ = a − ib.
- **Modulus** |z| = √(a² + b²).
- z·z̄ = a² + b² = |z|².
- **Multiplicative inverse** z⁻¹ = z̄/|z|² (z ≠ 0).
- Properties: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|, |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|, conj(z₁ ± z₂) = z̄₁ ± z̄₂, conj(z₁z₂) = z̄₁z̄₂.

steps.title: Solved example 1: division
steps.body:
Express (5 + √2 i)/(1 − √2 i) as a + ib.

- Multiply by (1 + √2 i)/(1 + √2 i).
- Numerator: 5 + 5√2 i + √2 i + 2i² = 3 + 6√2 i.
- Denominator: 1 + 2 = 3.
- Result: **1 + 2√2 i**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing |a + ib| = a + b or √(a² − b²).
- Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate.
- Writing z⁻¹ = z̄ (true only when |z| = 1).

steps.title: Shortcut
steps.body: If z = (a + ib)/(c + id), then |z| = √(a² + b²)/√(c² + d²) — no need to simplify first.

activity.prompt: Match z with |z|.

quiz.why: (3 − 2i)i = 3i − 2i² = 3i + 2 = 2 + 3i. Its conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part: 2 − 3i.
|a + bi| = √(a² + b²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The modulus is not 7, which is a sum of absolute values.
1/i = i/i² = i/(−1) = −i. Multiplying top and bottom by i removes i from the denominator.
z·z̄ = a² + b² = 4² + (−3)² = 16 + 9 = 25. This is |z|², a real number.
Multiply top and bottom by (1 + i): (1 + i)²/((1 − i)(1 + i)) = 2i/2 = i.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations)

lessons.title: Argand plane and polar form

scenes.text: Argand's idea: plot a + ib as the point (a, b). Real numbers sit on the x-axis, imaginary ones on the y-axis.
Now each complex number has a distance from the origin and a direction — like a compass bearing.

steps.title: Argand plane
steps.body:
The point P(a, b) represents z = a + ib. The x-axis is the **real axis**, the y-axis the **imaginary axis**.

- |z| = OP, the distance from the origin.
- z̄ = a − ib is the mirror image of P in the real axis.
- |z₁ − z₂| is the distance between the points z₁ and z₂.

steps.title: Polar form
steps.body:
With r = |z| and angle θ from the positive real axis: a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ, so
**z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)**.

θ is an **argument** of z. The **principal argument** lies in (−π, π]. Find the reference angle α = tan⁻¹|b/a| and place it in the correct quadrant.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Write z = 1 + i√3 in polar form.

- r = √(1 + 3) = 2.
- cos θ = 1/2, sin θ = √3/2 → θ = π/3 (QI).
- z = **2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3)**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Write z = −1 + i in polar form.

- r = √2. Reference angle α = π/4.
- Point (−1, 1) is in QII, so θ = π − π/4 = 3π/4.
- z = **√2(cos 3π/4 + i sin 3π/4)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking θ = tan⁻¹(b/a) without checking the quadrant: −1 − i has argument −3π/4, not π/4.
- Giving r as negative — the modulus is always ≥ 0.
- Forgetting that arguments differ by multiples of 2π.

activity.prompt: Which quadrant of the Argand plane?

quiz.why: −1 − i lies in the third quadrant, with reference angle π/4. The principal argument is taken in (−π, π], so it is −3π/4 (not 5π/4).

quiz.q: The conjugate of z is its reflection in the
quiz.why: The conjugate x − iy changes the sign of the imaginary part, so it is the mirror image of z in the real axis.
cos π/2 = 0 and sin π/2 = 1, so 2(0 + i·1) = 2i.

lessons.title: Quadratic equations with complex roots

scenes.text: An engineer's equation x² + 2x + 5 = 0 has a negative discriminant.
Its roots −1 ± 2i are not 'errors'; they describe an oscillating current that slowly dies down.

steps.title: Solving when D < 0
steps.body:
For ax² + bx + c = 0 with real a, b, c (a ≠ 0) and D = b² − 4ac:
- D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: equal real roots;
- **D < 0:** no real roots; roots are **x = (−b ± i√(4ac − b²))/(2a)**, a conjugate pair.

A polynomial equation of degree n has n roots (counted with multiplicity).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing √(−19) = −√19 instead of i√19.
- Forgetting the 2a in the denominator under both terms.
- Expecting conjugate roots when coefficients are not real.
- Sum of roots is −b/a and product c/a — still true for complex roots; use it to check.

steps.title: Check your roots
steps.body: For x² + x + 1 = 0, the roots ω, ω̄ satisfy ω + ω̄ = −1 and ωω̄ = 1. Verify with the values above.

activity.prompt: Fill in for x² − 4x + 13 = 0.

quiz.why: x² + 9 = 0 gives x² = −9, so x = ±√−9 = ±3i. The real values ±3 do not satisfy it.

quiz.q: If D < 0 for a real quadratic, its roots are
quiz.why: When D < 0 and the coefficients are real, the roots are non-real and come in conjugate pairs. One real and one complex root is not possible.
D = b² − 4ac = 1 − 4(2)(1) = 1 − 8 = −7. A negative discriminant means complex roots.

quiz.q: The product of roots of 3x² − 2x + 5 = 0 is
quiz.why: For ax² + bx + c = 0, the product of roots is c/a = 5/3. The sum would be −b/a = 2/3.

questions.why: The magnitude of Z = 3 + 4i is |Z| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 ohms. It is not 7, which is simply 3 + 4.

questions.why: The modulus of a quotient is the quotient of moduli: |a + ib| = |a − ib|, so |x + iy| = 1. Therefore x² + y² = 1.

questions.q: The least positive integer n with ((1 + i)/(1 − i))ⁿ = 1 is
questions.why: (1 + i)/(1 − i) = (1 + i)²/2 = 2i/2 = i. Powers of i equal 1 first at i⁴, so n = 4.

questions.why: z₁ + z₂ + 1 = 4, and z₁ − z₂ + 1 = 2 − 2i. Its modulus is √(4 + 4) = 2√2, so the ratio is 4/(2√2) = √2.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Linear Inequalities
courses.summary: Rules for handling inequalities, solving linear inequalities in one variable with number-line answers, graphing inequalities in two variables, and systems of inequalities in word problems.
outcomes: Learners can apply the rules for adding to and multiplying both sides of an inequality
Learners can solve linear inequalities in one variable and show solutions on a number line

lessons.title: Inequalities and the rules that keep them true

scenes.text: Ananya has ₹500. Each guest's snack costs ₹40. 'At most' 500 means she needs 40x ≤ 500, not 40x = 500.
Real life is full of 'at least', 'at most', 'more than' — the language of inequalities.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
An **inequality** compares two expressions with <, >, ≤ or ≥.
- **Strict:** a < b, a > b. **Slack:** a ≤ b, a ≥ b.
- **Linear in one variable:** ax + b < 0 (a ≠ 0). **Linear in two variables:** ax + by ≥ c.
- **Quadratic:** ax² + bx + c ≤ 0 (not studied in detail here).

steps.title: Two rules
steps.body:
- **Rule 1:** adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the sign.
- **Rule 2:** multiplying or dividing both sides by the same **positive** number keeps the sign; by a **negative** number **reverses** it.

Example: −2x < 6 → x > −3 (divide by −2, flip).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Solve 5 − 3x ≥ 11 for real x.

- Subtract 5: −3x ≥ 6.
- Divide by −3 and reverse: x ≤ −2.
- Solution set (−∞, −2].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative number.
- Multiplying both sides by an expression like x whose sign is unknown.
- Using a closed dot for a strict inequality on the number line.

statements.s: If a < b, then a + 7 < b + 7.
statements.why: Adding the same number keeps the order.

statements.s: If a < b, then −a < −b.
If 3x > 12, then x > 4.
x ≤ 5 includes x = 5.
If a < b, then 1/a < 1/b for all non-zero a, b.
statements.why: For positive a, b it reverses: 2 < 3 but 1/2 > 1/3.

quiz.why: Divide both sides by −4. Dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality: x < −2.

quiz.q: Solution of x + 5 ≤ 2 in integers includes
quiz.why: x + 5 ≤ 2 gives x ≤ −3. Among the choices, only −3 satisfies this; −2, 0 and 3 are larger.
'At least 18' means 18 or more, so x ≥ 18. The strict sign x > 18 would exclude 18 itself.
3x < 5 gives x < 5/3 ≈ 1.67. Among natural numbers only 1 fits (0 is not a natural number here, and 2 is too big), so the solution set is {1}.

quiz.q: An inequality with ≥ or ≤ is called
quiz.why: Inequalities with ≤ or ≥ allow equality, and the textbook calls them slack (non-strict) inequalities. Strict inequalities use only < or >.

lessons.title: Solving one-variable inequalities and word problems

scenes.text: Ravi scored 70 and 75 in two tests. He needs an average of at least 60.
(70 + 75 + x)/3 ≥ 60 tells him the minimum score in the third test: 35.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- Clear fractions by multiplying by the LCM (positive).
- Collect x-terms on one side, constants on the other.
- Divide by the coefficient (flip if negative).
- Write the answer as a set or interval and show it on a number line: open circle for <, >; filled dot for ≤, ≥.

steps.title: Solved example 3: consecutive odd numbers
steps.body:
Find pairs of consecutive odd positive integers, both less than 10, with sum more than 11.

- Let them be x and x + 2: x + 2 < 10 → x < 8, and 2x + 2 > 11 → x > 4.5.
- Odd x with 4.5 < x < 8: x = 5, 7 → pairs **(5, 7) and (7, 9)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Splitting a compound inequality and forgetting to combine the answers.
- Ignoring the number type asked (natural, integer, real).
- Translating 'more than' as ≥.

activity.prompt: Ravi scored 70 and 75 in two tests. What is the minimum he must score in the third so that the average is at least 60?

quiz.why: Expand: 4x + 6 − 10 < 6x − 12, so 4x − 4 < 6x − 12. Moving terms gives 8 < 2x, so x > 4.
Subtract 4: −7 ≤ −7x/2 ≤ 14. Multiply by −2/7, which reverses both signs: 2 ≥ x ≥ −4, i.e. −4 ≤ x ≤ 2.
Multiply by 6: 2x > 3x + 6, so −x > 6. Multiplying by −1 reverses the sign, giving x < −6.

quiz.q: On a number line, x < 3 is shown with
options: a filled dot at 3 shading left
a filled dot at 3 shading right
an open circle at 3 shading right
an open circle at 3 and shading to the left
quiz.why: x < 3 excludes 3, so we draw an open circle at 3, and shade the numbers less than 3, which lie to the left. A filled dot would mean 3 is included.

quiz.q: A rectangle's length is 3 times its breadth and its perimeter is at least 160 cm. The breadth must be
quiz.why: Length = 3b, so perimeter = 2(3b + b) = 8b. Then 8b ≥ 160 gives b ≥ 20, so the breadth is at least 20 cm.

scenes.text: Pens cost ₹10 and notebooks ₹40. With at most ₹120, which (pens, notebooks) choices are possible?
Every allowed choice is a point in a shaded region of the plane: 10x + 40y ≤ 120.

steps.title: Graphing ax + by < c
steps.body:
- Draw the line ax + by = c: **dashed** for < or >, **solid** for ≤ or ≥.
- The line divides the plane into two **half-planes**.
- Test a point not on the line, usually (0, 0). If it satisfies the inequality, shade its side; otherwise shade the other side.
- x > 0 is the right half-plane; y ≥ 0 is on and above the x-axis.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Graph 3x + 2y > 6.

- Line 3x + 2y = 6 passes (2, 0) and (0, 3); draw it dashed.
- Test (0, 0): 0 > 6 is false.
- Shade the half-plane **not containing the origin**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Graph y ≤ 2x.

- Line y = 2x passes through the origin, so test (1, 0): 0 ≤ 2 true.
- Draw the line solid and shade the side containing (1, 0) (below-right of the line).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing (0, 0) when the line passes through the origin — choose another point.
- Using a solid line for a strict inequality.
- Shading the wrong side after the test fails.

steps.title: Try the Graph plotter
steps.body: Draw the boundary line in the Graph plotter lab and check test points before shading on paper.

Find two points: (2, 0) and (0, 4)

quiz.why: For a strict inequality like x + y < 5, points on the line do not satisfy it, so the boundary line is drawn dashed. A solid line is for ≤ or ≥.

lessons.title: Systems of linear inequalities and applications

scenes.text: A chemist has 640 L of 8% acid and wants a mix between 4% and 6% acid by adding 2% acid.
Two inequalities at once fix the range of litres she can add.

steps.title: System of inequalities
steps.body:
Solve each inequality and take the **common region** (intersection).
- One variable: intersect the intervals on a number line.
- Two variables: shade each half-plane; the overlap is the solution region (it may be empty, bounded or unbounded).

steps.title: Solved example 1: one variable
steps.body:
Solve 5x − 7 < 3(x + 3) and 1 − 3x/2 ≥ x − 4.

- First: 5x − 7 < 3x + 9 → x < 8.
- Second: multiply by 2: 2 − 3x ≥ 2x − 8 → 10 ≥ 5x → x ≤ 2.
- Common: **x ≤ 2**, i.e. (−∞, 2].

steps.title: Solved example 3: two variables
steps.body: Region for x + y ≤ 6, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0: the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 6) including its sides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the union of solution sets instead of the intersection.
- Dropping non-negativity conditions (x ≥ 0) in real-life problems.
- Arithmetic slips with percentages — write them as decimals first.

activity.prompt: Solve the system 2x − 1 > 5 and 3x + 2 ≤ 20. What is the largest integer solution?

quiz.q: Common solution of x > 2 and x ≤ 7 is
quiz.why: x > 2 gives (2, ∞) and x ≤ 7 gives (−∞, 7]. Their common part is (2, 7], with 2 excluded and 7 included.

quiz.q: The system x > 5 and x < 3 has
quiz.why: No number can be greater than 5 and also less than 3 at the same time, so the two conditions do not overlap and there is no solution.

quiz.q: The region x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 is a
quiz.why: The line x + y = 4 meets the axes at (4, 0) and (0, 4). With x, y ≥ 0 the region is the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 4).
Add 4 to all parts: 6 ≤ 3x ≤ 9. Dividing by 3 gives 2 ≤ x ≤ 3, with both ends included.

quiz.q: In word problems, quantities like 'number of items' usually also need
quiz.why: Counts of items cannot be negative, so word problems need non-negativity conditions such as x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 alongside the main inequalities.

questions.why: Multiplying both sides of an inequality by −1 reverses its direction. So x < 5 becomes −x > −5.

questions.q: Solution of 3x + 8 > 2 for real x is
questions.why: 3x + 8 > 2 gives 3x > −6, so x > −2. The interval is (−2, ∞), with −2 not included.
A square bracket means the endpoint is included and a round one means excluded. So [−3, 4) is −3 ≤ x < 4.
4x + 3 < 5x + 7 gives 3 − 7 < 5x − 4x, so −4 < x, which is x > −4.
−2 < x ≤ 1 excludes −2 and includes 1, so the integers are −1, 0 and 1.
Multiply by 6: 2(x − 1) ≥ 3(x + 1), so 2x − 2 ≥ 3x + 3. This gives −5 ≥ x, i.e. x ≤ −5.
The inequality 2x + 3y ≥ 12 includes equality, so points on the line satisfy it and the boundary is drawn solid.

questions.q: Assertion: The solution of 2x > 3x is x < 0. Reason: Subtracting 3x from both sides gives −x > 0.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Subtracting 3x from both sides of 2x > 3x gives −x > 0, and multiplying by −1 reverses the sign to x < 0, so R is the very step that gives A.

questions.q: The set of x satisfying both 3x − 7 > 2(x − 6) and 6 − x > 11 − 2x is
questions.why: First: 3x − 7 > 2x − 12 gives x > −5. Second: 6 − x > 11 − 2x gives x > 5. Both hold only when x > 5, so the solution is (5, ∞).

questions.q: Which point lies in the region x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0?
questions.why: Check each point: (2, 3) gives 2 + 6 = 8 ≤ 8 with x, y ≥ 0, so it fits. (9, 0) gives 9 > 8, (4, 3) gives 10 > 8 and (−1, 1) has negative x.

questions.q: Case: A company makes x units; cost C = 26000 + 30x and revenue R = 43x. To make a profit, x must exceed
questions.why: Profit needs revenue > cost: 43x > 26000 + 30x, so 13x > 26000 and x > 2000. The company must make more than 2000 units.

questions.q: Case: In an experiment, a solution must be kept between 68°F and 77°F. The range in Celsius (F = 9C/5 + 32) is
questions.why: 68 < 9C/5 + 32 < 77 gives 36 < 9C/5 < 45. Multiplying by 5/9 gives 20 < C < 25, so the range is 20°C to 25°C.
|x − 2| < 3 means −3 < x − 2 < 3. Adding 2 gives −1 < x < 5, i.e. the interval (−1, 5).

questions.q: Case: IQ = (MA/CA) × 100. For 12-year-olds with 80 ≤ IQ ≤ 140, the mental age MA lies in
questions.why: IQ = MA/12 × 100, so 80 ≤ 100·MA/12 ≤ 140. Multiplying by 12/100 gives 9.6 ≤ MA ≤ 16.8 years.

questions.q: How many litres of water must be added to 1125 L of a 45% acid solution so that the result contains more than 25% but less than 30% acid?
The number of integer points (x, y) with x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 and x + y ≤ 3 is
questions.why: For x + y = 0, 1, 2, 3 there are 1, 2, 3, 4 non-negative integer points respectively. Total = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Permutations and Combinations
courses.summary: The fundamental principle of counting, factorials, permutations with and without repetition and with identical objects, combinations and their properties, and mixed selection–arrangement problems.
outcomes: Learners can apply the multiplication principle
Learners can compute nPr and arrangements of objects that are not all distinct
Learners can compute nCr and use its properties
Learners can decide when order matters and solve mixed problems

scenes.text: A school locker uses a 3-digit code. Mohit wonders how long a thief would need to try every code.
10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 codes. Counting by multiplying stages is the fundamental principle.

steps.title: Multiplication principle
steps.body:
If one event can occur in m ways and, after it, another independent event in n ways, then both together can occur in **m × n** ways. This extends to any number of stages.

**Addition principle:** if a task can be done in m ways OR (exclusively) in n ways, it can be done in m + n ways.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
How many 3-digit even numbers can be formed from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 if digits can repeat?

- Units place must be even: 3 choices (2, 4, 6).
- Tens: 6 choices; hundreds: 6 choices.
- Total = 6 × 6 × 3 = **108**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
How many signals can be made with 2 distinct flags hung one below the other from 5 different flags?

- Top: 5 choices; bottom: 4 (no repetition).
- Total = **20** signals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Filling an unrestricted place first and running out of choices for a restricted one — always fill restricted places first.
- Multiplying when cases are alternatives (should add).
- Allowing 0 as the first digit of a number.

activity.prompt: How many 4-letter codes (letters may repeat) can be made from the 26 English letters? Enter the count.

quiz.q: A person has 4 shirts and 3 trousers. Number of outfits:
quiz.why: By the multiplication principle, each of the 4 shirts can go with each of the 3 trousers, so 4 × 3 = 12 outfits. Adding would give 7, which is wrong because both choices are made.

quiz.q: Number of 2-digit numbers with distinct digits from 1–5 is
quiz.why: The tens digit can be chosen in 5 ways, and the units digit in 4 ways (it must differ). So 5 × 4 = 20 numbers.
Each of the 5 questions has 2 possible answers, so the total is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁵ = 32.

quiz.q: Number of 3-digit numbers (no restriction other than first digit ≠ 0) is
quiz.why: The first digit has 9 choices (1–9), and each of the other two digits has 10 choices. So 9 × 10 × 10 = 900.

quiz.q: A trip can go by 3 buses or 2 trains (one mode). Ways:
quiz.why: The trip uses one mode only, either a bus or a train, so we add: 3 + 2 = 5. Multiplying is for steps done one after another.

scenes.text: Eight runners, three medals: gold, silver, bronze.
Order matters on a podium — that makes it a permutation: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 results.

steps.title: Factorial and nPr
steps.body:
**n! = 1 × 2 × … × n**, with 0! = 1.

A **permutation** is an arrangement in a definite order. The number of permutations of n different objects taken r at a time (no repetition):
**ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!**, 0 ≤ r ≤ n.

- ⁿPₙ = n!
- With repetition allowed: **nʳ**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
How many 4-digit numbers can be formed from 1–9 with no digit repeated?

- ⁹P₄ = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = **3024**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 0! = 0 (it is 1).
- Using ⁿPᵣ when repetition is allowed.
- (a + b)! ≠ a! + b!; (2n)! ≠ 2·n!.

activity.prompt: Match.

quiz.q: Number of arrangements of the letters of 'ROSE' is
quiz.why: The 4 different letters of ROSE can be arranged in 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways.

quiz.q: 3-letter 'words' from A, B, C, D, E with repetition allowed:
quiz.why: With repetition allowed, each of the 3 positions can hold any of the 5 letters, so there are 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 words.

quiz.q: Ways to seat 5 people in a row:
quiz.why: Five different people in 5 seats can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways.

lessons.title: Permutations with identical objects and conditions

scenes.text: A shop makes all arrangements of the letters of 'ALLAHABAD' for a puzzle.
Swapping two identical A's does not create a new arrangement — so we divide by the repeats.

steps.title: Identical objects
steps.body:
The number of permutations of n objects where p₁ are alike of one kind, p₂ alike of another, …:
**n!/(p₁! p₂! … pₖ!)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Arrangements of ALLAHABAD.

- 9 letters: A × 4, L × 2, H, B, D.
- 9!/(4! 2!) = 362880/48 = **7560**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: vowels together
steps.body:
In how many arrangements of DAUGHTER do the vowels come together?

- Vowels A, U, E form one block; with D, G, H, T, R that is 6 units: 6! = 720.
- Vowels arrange inside the block: 3! = 6.
- Total = **4320**.

Vowels never together = 8! − 4320 = 40320 − 4320 = 36000.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body: Arrangements of MISSISSIPPI: 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = **34650** (I × 4, S × 4, P × 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by the wrong factorials (count each repeated letter carefully).
- In 'together' problems forgetting to arrange within the block.
- Treating 'not together' as 'never adjacent' — use total minus together only when the group is treated as one block.

activity.prompt: How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters of the word 'BANANA'?

quiz.why: INDIA has 5 letters with I repeated twice, so the arrangements are 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60.

quiz.q: Arrangements of 'ASSASSINATION' contain the factor in the denominator
quiz.why: In ASSASSINATION, S appears 4 times, A 3 times, I twice and N twice. The repeats go in the denominator: 4! 3! 2! 2!.

quiz.q: Ways to arrange 3 red and 2 blue identical balls in a row:
quiz.why: Arranging 5 balls where 3 are alike and 2 are alike gives 5!/(3! 2!) = 120/12 = 10 ways.

quiz.q: Arrangements of 'BOOK' with the two O's together:
quiz.why: Treat the two O's as one block. Then B, OO, K are 3 items, which can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways; the two O's are identical so nothing more to multiply.

quiz.q: Number of 6-digit numbers from 1, 2, 0, 2, 4, 2 (all used) is
quiz.why: The digits 1, 2, 0, 2, 4, 2 have 2 repeated three times, so total arrangements = 6!/3! = 120. Those starting with 0 number 5!/3! = 20, so valid 6-digit numbers = 120 − 20 = 100.

scenes.text: A coach must pick 3 players out of 7 for a relay — no positions, just who is in.
Order does not matter, so it is a combination: ⁷C₃ = 35.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **combination** is a selection where order does not matter.

**ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!) = ⁿPᵣ/r!**

Properties:
- ⁿC₀ = ⁿCₙ = 1
- **ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ**
- ⁿCₐ = ⁿC_b ⇒ a = b or a + b = n
- **ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ** (Pascal's rule)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
If ⁿC₈ = ⁿC₂, find ⁿC₂.

- 8 + 2 = n → n = 10.
- ¹⁰C₂ = 10 × 9/2 = **45**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: diagonals
steps.body:
How many diagonals does a decagon have?

- Lines joining 2 of 10 vertices: ¹⁰C₂ = 45.
- Subtract the 10 sides: **35 diagonals**. In general n(n − 3)/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ⁿPᵣ when order does not matter (or vice versa). Ask: does swapping two chosen items give a new outcome?
- Computing ⁿCᵣ for large r directly — use ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ (e.g. ²⁰C₁₈ = ²⁰C₂ = 190).

activity.prompt: Does order matter?

items.text: Choosing 4 books to take on a trip

quiz.why: ⁸C₃ = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56. The 336 would be ⁸P₃, where order matters.

quiz.q: Number of handshakes among 12 people (each pair once):
quiz.why: A handshake is a pair of people and order does not matter, so the count is ¹²C₂ = (12 × 11)/2 = 66.
Pascal's rule says ⁿCᵣ₋₁ + ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ. With n = 5 and r = 3, ⁵C₂ + ⁵C₃ = ⁶C₃.

quiz.q: Number of triangles from 10 points, no three collinear:
quiz.why: Any 3 of the 10 points form a triangle when no three are collinear, so the number is ¹⁰C₃ = (10 × 9 × 8)/6 = 120.

scenes.text: A college forms a committee of 5 from 6 boys and 4 girls with exactly 2 girls.
Choose girls, choose boys, multiply: ⁴C₂ × ⁶C₃ = 120.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
- Read 'at least', 'at most', 'exactly' carefully and split into cases.
- **Select first** (combinations), then **arrange** (permutations) if order matters.
- 'At least one' is often easiest as total − none.

steps.title: Solved example 1: at least
steps.body:
Committee of 5 from 6 boys and 4 girls with at least 3 girls.

- 3 girls: ⁴C₃·⁶C₂ = 4·15 = 60
- 4 girls: ⁴C₄·⁶C₁ = 6
- Total = **66**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: words with selection
steps.body:
How many 'words' with 2 vowels and 3 consonants can be formed from the letters of INVOLUTE (vowels I, O, U, E; consonants N, V, L, T)?

- Select: ⁴C₂·⁴C₃ = 6·4 = 24.
- Arrange each selection of 5: 5! = 120.
- Total = **2880**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: cards
steps.body: Ways to choose 4 cards from a 52-card deck with all four of the same suit: 4 × ¹³C₄ = 4 × 715 = **2860**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing 'at least 1 girl' as ⁴C₁ × (rest from everyone) — this double counts.
- Forgetting to arrange after selecting when the question asks for words or numbers.
- Adding when you should multiply across independent stages.

activity.prompt: A team of 4 is chosen from 5 men and 3 women. In how many ways if the team has exactly 1 woman?

quiz.q: Ways to choose 2 boys from 5 and 1 girl from 3:
quiz.why: Choose 2 boys from 5 in ⁵C₂ = 10 ways and 1 girl from 3 in ³C₁ = 3 ways. Multiply for both choices: 10 × 3 = 30.

quiz.q: Committees of 3 from 8 people that include a particular person:
quiz.why: With one particular person already on the committee, choose the other 2 from the remaining 7: ⁷C₂ = 21.

quiz.q: Ways to choose at least one of 4 different books:
quiz.why: Each of the 4 books can be taken or left, giving 2⁴ = 16 selections. Removing the case of taking none leaves 16 − 1 = 15.

quiz.q: Number of 5-card hands with exactly one ace:
quiz.why: Choose the one ace from 4 in 4 ways, then the other 4 cards from the 48 non-aces in ⁴⁸C₄ ways. So the count is 4 × ⁴⁸C₄.

quiz.q: Selecting 3 from 6 and then arranging them in a row gives
quiz.why: Choosing 3 of 6 gives ⁶C₃ = 20 selections, and arranging each in 3! = 6 ways gives 120, which equals ⁶P₃ = 6 × 5 × 4.

questions.why: By definition, 0! = 1. This keeps formulas like ⁿCₙ = n!/(n! 0!) = 1 consistent.
⁶P₃ = 6 × 5 × 4 = 120, the number of ordered selections of 3 from 6.
⁹C₇ = ⁹C₂ because ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ. So it equals (9 × 8)/2 = 36.
APPLE has 5 letters with P repeated twice, so the arrangements are 5!/2! = 60.

questions.q: Number of 3-digit numbers with distinct digits is
questions.why: The first digit has 9 choices (not 0), the second has 9 (any except the first, including 0) and the third has 8. So 9 × 9 × 8 = 648.
ⁿC₉ = ⁿC₈ means 9 + 8 = n, so n = 17. Then ¹⁷C₁₇ = 1.

questions.q: Ways to choose 2 of 10 points to draw lines (no three collinear):
questions.why: A line is fixed by choosing 2 points and order does not matter, so ¹⁰C₂ = (10 × 9)/2 = 45.

questions.q: Assertion: The number of ways to choose 3 of 5 objects equals the number of ways to choose 2 of 5. Reason: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Because ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, choosing 3 of 5 to take is the same as choosing the 2 to leave behind, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Arrangements of 'PERMUTATIONS' starting with P and ending with S:
questions.why: PERMUTATIONS has 12 letters. With P first and S last, 10 letters remain to arrange in the middle, and T repeats twice, giving 10!/2!.

questions.q: Ways to seat 6 people in a row if two particular people must sit together:
questions.why: Treat the two people as a block, so there are 5 units to arrange: 5! = 120. The pair can swap in 2! ways, so total = 120 × 2 = 240.

questions.q: Number of diagonals in a polygon with 12 sides:
questions.why: An n-sided polygon has n(n − 3)/2 diagonals. For n = 12, that is 12 × 9/2 = 54. (¹²C₂ = 66 also counts the 12 sides.)

questions.q: Case: A quiz has 10 questions in two parts of 5 each. A student must attempt 8, with at least 3 from each part. Number of ways:
questions.why: With 8 questions and at least 3 from each part of 5, the splits are (3, 5), (4, 4) and (5, 3). Counts: 10 × 1 + 5 × 5 ... precisely ⁵C₃·⁵C₅ = 10, ⁵C₄·⁵C₄ = 25, ⁵C₅·⁵C₃ = 10, total 45.

questions.q: Number of 4-digit numbers > 5000 from digits 0, 1, 3, 5, 7 without repetition:
questions.why: To exceed 5000 the first digit must be 5 or 7, giving 2 ways. The remaining 3 places use the other 4 digits in ⁴P₃ = 24 ways, so 2 × 24 = 48.

questions.q: Ways to arrange the letters of 'EXAMINATION' with vowels in the odd positions (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11)?
questions.why: 6 vowels E, A, A, I, I, O fill 6 odd places: 6!/(2!2!); 5 consonants X, M, N, T, N fill even places: 5!/2!.

questions.q: Number of ways 5 boys and 3 girls can sit in a row so that no two girls are together:
questions.why: Seat the 5 boys first in 5! ways. This leaves 6 gaps (including the ends), and the 3 girls take 3 different gaps in ⁶P₃ ways, so no two girls sit together.
By Pascal's rule, ⁿ⁻¹C₃ + ⁿ⁻¹C₄ = ⁿC₄. Then ⁿC₄ > ⁿC₃ means (n − 3)/4 > 1, so n > 7.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Binomial Theorem
courses.summary: Pascal's triangle, the binomial theorem for positive integral index, expansions and approximations, general and middle terms, and simple applications to divisibility and comparison.
outcomes: Learners can state and use the binomial theorem
Learners can expand (a + b)ⁿ and simplify special cases
Learners can find a specific term, the middle term and the term independent of x
Learners can use expansions for divisibility and estimation

scenes.text: In an art class, Zoya stacks numbers where each is the sum of the two above it: 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1 …
She has rebuilt Pascal's triangle — a pattern described centuries earlier in Indian tradition as Meru Prastara — and its rows are the coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ.

steps.title: Pascal's triangle
steps.body:
Row n gives the coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ:
- n = 0: 1
- n = 1: 1 1
- n = 2: 1 2 1
- n = 3: 1 3 3 1
- n = 4: 1 4 6 4 1
- n = 5: 1 5 10 10 5 1

Each entry is ⁿCᵣ, and Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ₋₁ + ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ builds the next row.

steps.title: Binomial theorem
steps.body:
For a positive integer n:
**(a + b)ⁿ = ⁿC₀aⁿ + ⁿC₁aⁿ⁻¹b + ⁿC₂aⁿ⁻²b² + … + ⁿCₙbⁿ**

- n + 1 terms.
- Powers of a fall from n to 0; powers of b rise from 0 to n; each term's powers add to n.
- Coefficients ⁿCᵣ are **binomial coefficients**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- (a + b)ⁿ ≠ aⁿ + bⁿ.
- Forgetting to raise the coefficient (e.g. 2 in 2y) to the power.
- Writing n terms instead of n + 1.

activity.prompt: Row 6 of Pascal's triangle.

quiz.q: Number of terms in (2x − y)⁷ is
quiz.why: (a + b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms. For n = 7, that gives 8 terms, not 7.

quiz.q: Coefficient of x² in (1 + x)⁵ is
quiz.why: The coefficient of x² in (1 + x)⁵ is ⁵C₂ = (5 × 4)/2 = 10.

quiz.q: Sum of the coefficients in row 5 of Pascal's triangle is
quiz.why: The numbers in row n of Pascal's triangle add up to 2ⁿ, so for row 5 the sum is 2⁵ = 32.
Expanding (a − b)³ with alternating signs gives a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³. The signs alternate because of the minus in the bracket.

quiz.q: In (a + b)ⁿ, the sum of powers of a and b in each term is
quiz.why: In each term of (a + b)ⁿ, as the power of a falls, the power of b rises, so together they always add up to n.

scenes.text: Can you compute 98⁵ without a calculator? Write it as (100 − 2)⁵.
Powers of 100 are easy, and the binomial theorem does the rest.

steps.title: Useful forms
steps.body:
- (x − y)ⁿ = Σ (−1)ʳ ⁿCᵣ xⁿ⁻ʳ yʳ (signs alternate).
- (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + ⁿC₁x + ⁿC₂x² + … + xⁿ.
- Put x = 1: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + … + ⁿCₙ = **2ⁿ**.
- Put x = −1: ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₂ − … = 0.

steps.title: Solved example 2: which is larger?
steps.body:
Which is larger, (1.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ or 10,000?

- (1 + 0.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ = 1 + 1000000(0.01) + (positive terms)
- = 1 + 10000 + … > 10000.
- So **(1.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ is larger**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the alternating signs in (a − b)ⁿ.
- Arithmetic slips with powers of 10 — line up place values.
- Using the approximation (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx when x is not small.

activity.prompt: Use (100 + 1)³ to compute 101³.

quiz.q: (1 + x)ⁿ at x = 1 gives the sum
quiz.why: Putting x = 1 in (1 + x)ⁿ gives 2ⁿ, which equals the sum of all the binomial coefficients.
This is the expansion of (1 − 1)ⁿ = 0ⁿ = 0, since the signs alternate. So the alternating sum of coefficients is 0.
In (a + b)⁴ − (a − b)⁴ the even-power terms cancel and the odd-power terms double: 2(4a³b + 4ab³) = 8a³b + 8ab³.

lessons.title: General term, middle term and independent term

scenes.text: An exam asks only for the coefficient of x⁶y³ in (x + 2y)⁹. Writing all 10 terms wastes time.
The general term formula jumps straight to the one you need.

steps.title: General term
steps.body:
In (a + b)ⁿ the (r + 1)th term is
**Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ**.

**Middle term(s):**
- n even: one middle term, T(n/2 + 1).
- n odd: two middle terms, T((n+1)/2) and T((n+3)/2).

**Term independent of x:** set the total power of x in Tᵣ₊₁ to 0 and solve for r.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Coefficient of x⁶y³ in (x + 2y)⁹.

- Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁹Cᵣ x⁹⁻ʳ(2y)ʳ; need r = 3.
- ⁹C₃ · 2³ = 84 × 8 = **672**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: middle term
steps.body:
Middle term of (x/3 + 9y)¹⁰.

- n = 10 even → T₆ (r = 5).
- ¹⁰C₅ (x/3)⁵ (9y)⁵ = 252 · 9⁵/3⁵ · x⁵y⁵ = 252 · 3⁵ x⁵y⁵ = **61236 x⁵y⁵**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: independent term
steps.body:
Term independent of x in (x² − 1/x)⁹.

- Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁹Cᵣ (x²)⁹⁻ʳ(−1/x)ʳ = (−1)ʳ ⁹Cᵣ x¹⁸⁻³ʳ.
- 18 − 3r = 0 → r = 6: (−1)⁶ ⁹C₆ = **84**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tᵣ₊₁ uses r, not r + 1, in ⁿCᵣ: the 4th term has r = 3.
- Forgetting the sign (−1)ʳ for (a − b)ⁿ.
- Confusing 'coefficient' with 'term' (the term includes the variables).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: Some rationalised editions treat general and middle terms lightly; they remain essential for competitive exams.

activity.prompt: Find the coefficient of x⁵ in (x + 3)⁸.

quiz.why: The (r + 1)th term is ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ. For the 4th term r = 3, so it is ⁷C₃ x⁴y³ = 35x⁴y³.

quiz.q: The number of middle terms in (a + b)⁹ is
quiz.why: (a + b)⁹ has 10 terms, which is an even count, so there are two middle terms, the 5th and 6th. A single middle term occurs only when n is even.
(1 + x)⁸ has 9 terms, so the middle one is the 5th: ⁸C₄ x⁴ = 70x⁴.

quiz.q: Term independent of x in (x + 1/x)⁶ is
quiz.why: The general term is ⁶Cᵣ x⁶⁻ʳ (1/x)ʳ = ⁶Cᵣ x⁶⁻²ʳ. Setting 6 − 2r = 0 gives r = 3, so the constant term is ⁶C₃ = 20.
The x² term uses r = 2: ⁵C₂(−2x)² = 10 × 4x² = 40x². The coefficient is 40 (positive, since the square removes the sign).

scenes.text: Today is Thursday. What day will it be after 8¹⁰ days?
8 = 7 + 1, so 8¹⁰ = (7 + 1)¹⁰ = (multiple of 7) + 1. It will be Friday!

steps.title: The idea
steps.body: Write the base as (multiple of m) ± 1 and expand: all terms except the last contain m. So the remainder appears immediately.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Show 6ⁿ − 5n leaves remainder 1 when divided by 25.

- 6ⁿ = (1 + 5)ⁿ = 1 + 5n + ⁿC₂·5² + ⁿC₃·5³ + …
- 6ⁿ − 5n = 1 + 25(ⁿC₂ + ⁿC₃·5 + …) = 1 + 25k.
- Remainder **1** ∎

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Remainder when 2³⁰ is divided by 7?

- 2³⁰ = (2³)¹⁰ = 8¹⁰ = (7 + 1)¹⁰ = 7k + 1.
- Remainder **1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping the expansion too early and missing a term not divisible by m.
- For (m − 1)ⁿ, the last term is (−1)ⁿ: the remainder depends on whether n is odd or even (use m − 1 for −1).

steps.title: Where it is used
steps.body: Probability (binomial distribution), compound interest approximations, computer science (counting subsets) and cryptography rest on these expansions.

activity.prompt: What is the remainder when 9¹⁰⁰ is divided by 8?

quiz.q: The remainder when 4ⁿ (n ≥ 1) is divided by 3 is
quiz.why: 4ⁿ = (3 + 1)ⁿ. Every term of the expansion except the last (1ⁿ = 1) has a factor of 3, so the remainder on dividing by 3 is 1.
The sum of all coefficients is 2ⁿ, and ⁿC₀ = 1 is missing from this sum. So it equals 2ⁿ − 1.

quiz.q: The last term in the expansion of (10 + 1)⁹ is
quiz.why: The last term of (a + b)ⁿ is bⁿ. For (10 + 1)⁹ that is 1⁹ = 1.
The sums of even-position and odd-position coefficients are equal, since (1 + 1)ⁿ = 2ⁿ and (1 − 1)ⁿ = 0. So each is half of 2ⁿ, i.e. 2ⁿ⁻¹.
Write 9ⁿ = (1 + 8)ⁿ = 1 + 8n + 64(ⁿC₂ + 8ⁿC₃ + …). So 9ⁿ − 8n − 1 has a factor 64, which makes it always divisible by 64.

questions.q: Number of terms in (x + y)¹² is
questions.why: A binomial expansion (x + y)ⁿ has n + 1 terms, so for n = 12 there are 13 terms.

questions.q: Coefficient of x³ in (1 + x)⁶ is
questions.why: The coefficient of x³ in (1 + x)⁶ is ⁶C₃ = (6 × 5 × 4)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 20.

questions.q: Sum of binomial coefficients in (1 + x)¹⁰ is
questions.why: The binomial coefficients of (1 + x)ⁿ add up to 2ⁿ. For n = 10, the sum is 2¹⁰ = 1024.
The 3rd term has r = 2: ⁵C₂ · 2³ · x² = 10 × 8 x² = 80x².
In (x + 1)⁴ + (x − 1)⁴ the odd-power terms cancel, leaving 2(x⁴ + 6x² + 1) = 2x⁴ + 12x² + 2.
(x − 1/x)¹⁰ has 11 terms, so the middle term is the 6th: ¹⁰C₅ x⁵(−1/x)⁵ = −252, as (−1)⁵ is negative and the x powers cancel.

questions.why: Both are true. By the binomial theorem, (1 + 0.1)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ > 1 + 10000(0.1) = 1001, which is more than 1000, so the reason explains the assertion.
The x⁵ term in (x + 3)⁸ uses 3³: ⁸C₃ × 3³ = 56 × 27 = 1512.

questions.q: Term independent of x in (2x − 1/x)⁶ is
questions.why: General term: ⁶Cᵣ(2x)⁶⁻ʳ(−1/x)ʳ has x⁶⁻²ʳ, so r = 3 gives the constant term ⁶C₃ · 2³ · (−1)³ = 20 × 8 × (−1) = −160.

questions.q: The remainder when 7¹⁰³ is divided by 6 is
questions.why: Write 7¹⁰³ = (6 + 1)¹⁰³. Every term except the last (1¹⁰³ = 1) has a factor of 6, so the remainder is 1.

questions.q: Case: A coin is tossed 6 times. The number of outcome sequences with exactly 2 heads equals the coefficient of x² in (1 + x)⁶, which is
questions.why: The number of sequences with exactly 2 heads in 6 tosses is the number of ways to choose which 2 tosses are heads: ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5)/2 = 15, which is the coefficient of x² in (1 + x)⁶.

questions.q: If the coefficients of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th terms of (1 + x)ⁿ are in A.P., n =
questions.why: The coefficients of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th terms are ⁿC₁, ⁿC₂, ⁿC₃. A.P. means 2ⁿC₂ = ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₃, which simplifies to n² − 9n + 14 = 0, giving n = 7 (n = 2 is too small to have a 4th term).

questions.q: The coefficient of a⁴ in (1 + a)⁴(1 − a)⁴ is
questions.why: (1 + a)⁴(1 − a)⁴ = (1 − a²)⁴. The a⁴ term comes from (−a²)², so its coefficient is ⁴C₂ = 6.

questions.q: The binomial coefficient of the 3rd term of (a + b)⁹ is
questions.why: The (r + 1)th term has binomial coefficient ⁿCᵣ. For the 3rd term r = 2, so the coefficient is ⁹C₂ = (9 × 8)/2 = 36.

questions.q: The greatest coefficient in (1 + x)¹⁰ is
questions.why: The greatest coefficient in (1 + x)¹⁰ is the middle one, ¹⁰C₅ = 252. Coefficients rise up to the middle and fall afterwards.

questions.q: If the coefficient of x in (x² + k/x)⁵ is 270, then k =
questions.why: The general term is ⁵Cᵣ(x²)⁵⁻ʳ(k/x)ʳ = ⁵Cᵣ kʳ x¹⁰⁻³ʳ. For x¹ we need r = 3, so ⁵C₃k³ = 10k³ = 270, giving k³ = 27 and k = 3.
